name: Yes/No Complement Arbitrage
description: Every binary market has a Yes share and a No share that should always add up to exactly $1.00, since one of them is guaranteed to be worth $1 at resolution. When the two prices instead add up to more than $1.00, you sell both sides (or short the overpriced pair) and pocket the difference no matter how the event turns out. The profit is locked in the moment you fill both legs; it just takes patience to hold until the market resolves.
requirements: Real-time order book scanner across all binary markets
Enough capital to hold both sides until market resolves
Low-latency execution to capture the spread before it closes

name: Cross-Market Arbitrage (Related Events)
description: Find two or more markets whose outcomes are logically connected, then trade the gap between their prices when the math doesn't line up. For example, a candidate can't win the general election without first winning the primary, so 'wins general' can never be priced higher than 'wins primary' times the chance of winning given the nomination. When the crowd violates that relationship, you buy the cheap leg and sell the rich one. The edge is the inconsistency between linked prices, not a view on who actually wins.
requirements: Model of the conditional probability between the linked markets
Automated price monitoring across multiple market URLs
Capital allocation rules to avoid correlated downside

name: Cross-Platform Arbitrage
description: The same real-world event is often traded on several venues at once (Polymarket, Kalshi, Betfair, sportsbooks). When one venue implies a meaningfully different probability than another, you buy the cheap side on one platform and sell the equivalent on the other, locking in the gap. The edge comes from price differences across markets that should agree; you must convert each venue's odds to a true probability after fees and the bookmaker's built-in margin (the 'vig').
requirements: Accounts and funded balances on at least two venues
Odds-conversion tooling that accounts for fees and vig
Awareness of regional/legal restrictions on each platform

name: Sportsbook-to-Polymarket Spread
description: Major-sport betting lines from big sportsbooks are extremely accurate because huge money keeps them honest, so they act as a reliable 'fair price.' This strategy treats the consensus sportsbook number as the truth and buys or sells the matching Polymarket market whenever Polymarket strays far from it. The edge is simply that Polymarket sports prices lag or overshoot the much sharper book line, and you collect the difference.
requirements: Live feed from 2+ sportsbook odds APIs (e.g., The Odds API)
Conversion script from American/decimal odds to probability
Threshold rules for minimum edge after gas/fees

name: Multi-Outcome Overround Shorting (Dutch-Book Lay)
description: In a market with several mutually-exclusive outcomes (only one can win, like 'Who wins the nomination'), add up the YES prices of every candidate. If they total more than $1, the market is overpriced as a whole. You bet against each candidate (buy the NO share on every one), and since exactly one wins, your basket of NOs is guaranteed to pay out more than it cost. The edge is that retail traders overpay across many fragmented candidate listings that nobody re-adds back to a clean 100%.
requirements: CLOB depth feed across all outcome tokens of a market group
Solver that sums NO-leg costs and flags basket < $1 net
Capital sized to fill all legs simultaneously before quotes move
Gas/slippage model to confirm net edge after fees

name: Split/Merge Redemption Arbitrage (CTF)
description: Every YES and NO pair on Polymarket can be created or redeemed for exactly $1 on-chain (the Conditional Token Framework, or CTF). When the YES and NO sell prices add up to LESS than $1, you mint a fresh $1 pair for collateral and sell both halves on the order book for more than $1. When they add up to MORE than $1, you buy both cheap and redeem the pair for a clean $1. The edge is the gap between the fixed $1 on-chain value and the live order-book prices, after gas.
requirements: CTF splitPosition/mergePositions contract calls
Live YES+NO best-ask/bid feed per market
Polygon gas + USDC approval automation
Latency budget under quote refresh interval

name: Kalshi-Polymarket Identical-Contract Relative Value
description: The same real-world question (a CPI inflation print, a Fed rate decision, an election result) is often listed on both Kalshi (a US-regulated exchange) and Polymarket (crypto-based). When the two venues disagree on the price, you buy the cheaper side on one and bet against it on the other, then hold both until they settle. Because one of them must be right, you lock in the difference. The edge is that the two platforms have separate, segmented user bases that keep prices out of line.
requirements: Kalshi API + Polymarket CLOB feed with contract-mapping table
Resolution-criteria reconciliation to confirm payouts match
Capital on both venues incl. USDC and USD funding
FX/fee/withdrawal-timing cost model

name: Betfair Lay vs. Polymarket Back Cross-Venue Lock
description: Some sports and politics events appear on both Betfair Exchange and Polymarket. You bet on the outcome at whichever venue is cheaper and bet against the same outcome on the other (on Betfair this is called 'laying'), after converting Betfair's decimal odds into a probability so the two prices are comparable. Holding both to the result locks in the spread. The edge is the price gap between a traditional exchange and an on-chain order book whose audiences and reaction speeds differ.
requirements: Betfair Exchange API + Polymarket feed with odds normalization
Event/outcome matching incl. resolution-rule parity check
Bankroll on both venues with commission accounting
Fast re-quote to avoid one-legged exposure

name: Settlement-Timing Funding Arbitrage
description: A market that is nearly certain often trades a bit under $1 (say $0.97) because it won't officially settle for months, and crypto traders dislike tying up cash that long. This strategy buys those near-sure things and treats the gap to $1 as interest earned over the wait, always rotating capital into whichever near-certain market offers the best annualized return. The edge is that the platform's settlement waits as resolved by its oracle (UMA) are underpriced as a cost-of-carry.
requirements: Feed of price + expected-resolution-timestamp per market
Annualized-yield ranking engine across the late-stage book
USDC opportunity-cost / DeFi benchmark rate
Patience and capital to hold to settlement

name: Triangular Arbitrage Across Linked Markets
description: Some markets are logically linked: for example 'A wins overall', 'A wins region R', and 'region R goes A's way' must obey the rule that the chance of A overall equals the chance A wins R times the chance R happens. When the separately-listed prices break this rule, you buy the underpriced combination and sell the overpriced pieces so the trade pays for itself. The edge is that nobody checks whether these related markets stay consistent with each other.
requirements: Dependency graph linking conditional/marginal markets
Probability-consistency solver flagging chain-rule violations
Multi-leg simultaneous execution bot
Mapping of resolution sources to confirm logical linkage

name: Polymarket-vs-Sportsbook Options-Style Synthetic RV
description: A Polymarket yes/no contract pays $1 if an event happens. You can rebuild that same payout synthetically using other instruments, like a sportsbook parlay or a crypto options spread that pays off in the same scenario. When the cost of building the payout that way differs from Polymarket's price for the same outcome, you buy the cheap version and sell the expensive one. The edge is pricing inconsistencies between fixed yes/no markets and continuous derivative markets.
requirements: Options/sportsbook pricing feed for replicable underlyings
Replication engine mapping binaries to spreads/digitals
Capital across derivative venue + Polymarket
Greeks/margin and resolution-mismatch risk model

name: Cross-Market Mutually-Exclusive Sum-Over-One Fade
description: Sometimes Polymarket lists several related markets that together cover all possibilities and can't both happen (e.g. separate 'BTC tops $X' tiers), but they aren't formally grouped, so nothing forces their prices to add to 100%. When their YES prices total more than $1, you bet against the whole overpriced set by buying NO on each tier. The edge is the missing 100% constraint across markets that the platform never linked together.
requirements: Semantic grouping of related-but-ungrouped markets
Mutual-exclusivity / exhaustiveness validator
Multi-leg NO execution with sum-cost monitoring
Resolution-overlap audit to rule out double-pay risk

name: Pre-Resolution Oracle-Lag Lock-In
description: When a real-world event is already decided but Polymarket's oracle (UMA) hasn't officially posted and finalized the result yet, the winning side can still be bought below $1. This strategy buys the winner (and the loser's NO) during that proposal-and-dispute lag, locking in the soon-to-be-confirmed payout. The edge is the delay between what actually happened and when the chain marks it official.
requirements: Authoritative real-world result feed faster than UMA proposal
UMA proposal/dispute-window state monitor per market
Capital and fast fills before book reprices to $1/$0
Dispute-risk filter for ambiguous resolution sources

name: Calendar Roll Arbitrage Across Serial Markets
description: The same underlying often has markets at different deadlines (e.g. 'BTC above $X by end of June' vs 'by end of July'). The later deadline should always be at least as likely as the earlier one. When the prices across these expiries don't line up logically, you buy the underpriced deadline and bet against the overpriced one. The edge is mispriced incremental probability between adjacent timeframes.
requirements: Term-structure dataset of serial markets on each underlying
No-arbitrage monotonicity checker across expiries
Two-leg execution and roll-management bot
Carry/funding model for holding the calendar spread

name: Gas-Fee Threshold Arbitrage
description: Some cross-venue and on-chain arbitrage spreads are genuinely profitable but only when Polygon gas is cheap; once gas spikes, the spread no longer covers transaction cost. Monitor Polygon's base fee and fire these marginal arbs only during low-gas windows, capturing spreads that competitors skip whenever gas is high. The edge is treating gas as a live, tradable cost input rather than a fixed friction you ignore.
requirements: Polygon base-fee/mempool monitor with EIP-1559 prediction
Gas-cost-net spread calculator per arb leg
Pre-signed transaction queue for instant low-gas firing
Capital staged on-chain to avoid bridge latency

name: Merge/Split Set-Completion Arbitrage
description: Polymarket's underlying contract lets you split $1.00 of collateral into a matched Yes+No pair, or merge a Yes+No pair back into $1.00. When you can buy Yes and No together for under $1.00 (or split collateral and sell both legs for over $1.00), run the mint/merge round-trip for a riskless spread after gas. The edge is exploiting the collateral primitive directly, not just complementary prices on the order book.
requirements: ConditionalTokens split/merge integration on Polygon
Simultaneous two-leg book monitor for the condition
Gas-net spread gate + atomic execution path
USDC float for collateral splitting

name: Resolution-Source Scrape-to-Order First-Mover
description: Poll the exact data source named in a market's resolution rule, a specific government CSV, an official results page, a CME settlement print, and fire your order the instant that canonical number updates, before traders relying on slower news catch on. The edge is sitting directly on the feed the oracle itself uses to settle, so you see the answer first.
requirements: Per-market mapping of resolution rule to the exact canonical URL/API
Sub-second change-detection poller with diff alerting
Pre-staged signed orders on Polymarket CLOB for instant submit
Legal review that the source's ToS permits polling

name: Block-Confirmation Race for On-Chain-Resolved Markets
description: For markets that settle on a verifiable on-chain event, a contract balance crossing a level, a governance vote passing, a block-height or halving milestone, watch the mempool and pending chain state so you can trade the near-certain outcome before the confirming block is mined and the market reprices. The edge is reading pending blockchain state a few seconds ahead of confirmation.
requirements: Mempool + pending-state node access on the relevant chain(s)
Decoder mapping target contract events to market resolution
Fast Polymarket order submission keyed to pending-tx detection
Reorg-risk guard sizing for non-finalized states

name: Season-Futures vs Game-by-Game Coherence
description: A season win-total market and the individual game markets for the same team describe the same reality, so the sum of the game probabilities has to line up with the futures price. Traders in the two markets rarely overlap, and the futures market updates slowly. You compute the implied win total from the game ladder and trade the futures market whenever the two disagree by more than a game — buying whichever side the more liquid, more frequently updated series supports.
requirements: Continuous aggregation of remaining game probabilities into an implied season total
Model of correlation between games so the sum isn't treated as independent
Capital patient enough to hold a futures position for the rest of the season

name: Field-Wide Overround Lay in Golf & Tennis
description: In a 156-player golf field, every player's win probability must sum to exactly 100%. In practice the listed prices sum to well above that, because long shots are systematically overpriced by people buying lottery tickets. You sell a broad basket of the most overpriced long shots simultaneously, capturing the excess. It requires real capital and strict correlation limits, since one of your shorts winning is exactly the scenario that hurts.
requirements: Full-field price capture with a running sum of implied probabilities
Capital to short many legs at once and margin for a long shot actually winning
Concentration limits so a single surprise winner cannot end the strategy

name: Fed-Funds Futures Implied-Path Import
description: The fed funds futures market prices the expected policy rate at every upcoming meeting, and billions of dollars of hedging keep it honest. Converting those contracts into a per-meeting cut or hike probability is arithmetic, not forecasting. Whenever Polymarket's rate-decision market disagrees with the futures-implied number by more than fees, you take the futures side — you are importing a far deeper market's consensus rather than forming a view on the economy.
requirements: CME fed funds and SOFR futures data with the standard implied-probability conversion
Handling for meeting-date mechanics and mid-month settlement conventions
Automated comparison and alerting when the two venues diverge

name: Breakeven & Inflation-Swap Import
description: The gap between nominal Treasury yields and inflation-protected ones — the breakeven rate — plus the inflation swap market give a continuously updated, professionally traded forecast of future inflation over any horizon. Polymarket's longer-dated inflation markets often price off narrative and recent prints instead. You convert the swap curve into a probability for each threshold market and trade the disagreement, adjusting for the small risk premium embedded in the bond spread.
requirements: TIPS breakeven and inflation-swap curve data across maturities
Adjustment for the inflation risk premium and seasonal carry in the swap curve
Conversion of a point forecast into a threshold probability using historical dispersion

name: Options Implied-Move Import for Stock Thresholds
description: The options market prices the exact same question as a stock threshold market: a digital option struck at $X expiring on date Y is, mathematically, the probability the stock finishes above $X. You read that probability directly from the option chain using the spread between adjacent strikes, then compare it to the Polymarket price. Where they diverge beyond fees you trade the gap, borrowing a market with orders of magnitude more capital behind it.
requirements: Live option chains with reliable bid/ask across strikes and expiries
Digital-probability extraction from strike spreads, adjusted for dividends and rates
Expiry-convention matching, since option settlement and market resolution differ

name: M&A Deal-Spread Completion Probability
description: When an acquisition is announced, the target trades below the offer price, and the size of that gap is the equity market's own estimate of the chance the deal closes. That estimate is made by specialists who read the merger agreement, the antitrust posture and the break-fee terms. You convert the spread into a completion probability and trade the Polymarket 'will the deal close' contract against it, adjusting for the expected time to closing.
requirements: Live target and acquirer prices plus the exact offer terms and any collar
Time-to-close estimate and discount rate to turn a spread into a probability
Regulatory docket monitoring for second requests and challenge filings

name: Strike-Ladder Monotonicity Arbitrage
description: Polymarket lists the same coin and date at several strikes — above $110k, above $120k, above $130k — and the prices have to fall as the strike rises, because clearing a higher bar is strictly harder. When two rungs cross or sit equal, the set is internally impossible and you can buy the cheaper-but-more-likely rung against the dearer one for a locked profit. No view on Bitcoin is required; the inconsistency is the trade.
requirements: Continuous scan of every strike in each coin-and-date family with monotonicity checks
Simultaneous two-leg execution so the violation cannot close between fills
Capital to hold both legs to resolution, since the lock only pays out at the end

name: Moneyline, Spread & Total Coherence Lock
description: For a single game the win market, the points-handicap market and the total-score market all describe one underlying distribution of results, so they cannot disagree freely. A team priced at 70% to win but only 45% to cover a small handicap implies a scoring distribution that does not exist. You fit the implied distribution across all three, find the leg that breaks it, and trade that leg against the others.
requirements: Joint scoring-distribution model per sport that ties win, handicap and total together
Simultaneous price capture across all related markets for the same game
Execution across several legs before the inconsistency is arbitraged away

name: Series-vs-Map Handicap Coherence
description: A best-of-three series and its map-handicap market are two views of the same thing: to win 2-0 you must win both maps, so the handicap price and the series price are linked by simple arithmetic once you assume a per-map win rate. Esports books frequently price the series carefully and the handicap lazily. You solve for the per-map rate implied by each and trade the leg whose implied rate is out of line.
requirements: Model linking per-map win probability to series and handicap prices for each format
Simultaneous capture of series, handicap and individual map markets
Adjustment for map-specific strength, since maps are not identically weighted

name: Temperature-Band Ladder Coherence
description: Daily temperature markets are usually listed as a ladder of bands or thresholds for the same city and day, and those prices must be internally consistent: the chance of exceeding 95°F can never be higher than the chance of exceeding 90°F, and mutually exclusive bands must sum to one. Weather markets are thin and are often priced band by band by different traders, so violations appear regularly. You scan the ladder and trade the breaks.
requirements: Full-ladder capture per city and day with monotonicity and sum-to-one checks
Multi-leg execution sized to the thinnest rung in the set
Verification that every rung resolves on the same station and the same definition

name: Seat-Count vs Individual-Race Coherence
description: A chamber-majority market and the individual seat markets that decide it are the same question at two levels of detail. Simulating the individual races — with a correlated national swing, because seats do not move independently — produces a majority probability that can be compared directly against the majority market's price. The two are traded by different crowds and drift apart regularly, especially when a handful of individual races reprice and the top-line market does not.
requirements: Simultaneous price capture across every competitive seat market and the majority market
Correlated simulation with a shared national-swing term, not independent seats
Multi-leg execution and capital to hold a long-dated majority position

name: Nested-Deadline Coherence Arbitrage
description: Geopolitical questions get listed at several horizons at once: will this happen by June, by September, by December. Those are nested — anything that happens by June has also happened by December — so the prices must rise with the horizon. Long-dated legs are thin and stale while the near-dated one reprices on every headline, which regularly pushes the set into impossibility. You buy the underpriced longer horizon against the overpriced shorter one.
requirements: Grouping of markets into nested-deadline families for the same underlying event
Monotonicity checks across horizons with alerting on violations
Patience and capital, since the lock resolves only at the longest horizon

name: Count-Bucket Ladder Arbitrage
description: Mention-count markets are listed as mutually exclusive buckets — 0 to 24 times, 25 to 49, 50 to 74, 75 or more — and exactly one of them must happen, so their prices must sum to one. In practice the exciting high bucket gets bid up while the boring middle ones go stale, and the set sums to well over one. You sell the whole overpriced set, or the specific rich bucket against the cheap ones, and collect the excess.
requirements: Bucket-set capture per figure and window with a running sum of implied probabilities
Multi-leg execution sized to the thinnest bucket in the set
Confirmation that the buckets are genuinely exhaustive and non-overlapping

name: Nominee-to-Winner Conditional Coherence
description: You cannot win an award you were not nominated for, so a 'wins Best Picture' market can never trade above the matching 'is nominated for Best Picture' market. Before nominations are announced both markets exist side by side, priced by people focused on the glamorous one, and the relationship breaks regularly. You buy the nomination leg against the win leg whenever the ordering inverts, which is a locked position regardless of who eventually wins.
requirements: Pairing of nomination and win markets for the same title and category
Ordering checks with alerting when the win price approaches or exceeds nomination
Understanding of category eligibility, which determines whether the pairing is valid

name: Mutually-Exclusive First-To-Ship Basket
description: Markets asking which company ships something first — a model above a benchmark, a consumer device, a regulatory approval — form a set where exactly one entrant can win, so the prices must sum to one. In practice the famous names get bid up individually with no one checking the total, and the set routinely sums well above one. You sell the whole overpriced basket, which pays regardless of which company actually wins the race.
requirements: Identification of genuinely exhaustive and exclusive entrant sets, including any 'none' outcome
Running sum of the field with alerting when the overround exceeds a threshold
Capital to short many legs at once and margin for the eventual winner

name: Indication-Nesting Coherence on Approval Markets
description: Drug markets nest: approval for a broad label implies approval, approval in a second indication implies approval in the first, and approval by June implies approval by December. Each of those is a strict subset relationship the prices must respect. Biotech markets are thin and are traded by people focused on the headline indication, so the narrower and broader legs regularly cross. You trade the pair rather than forecasting the science.
requirements: Mapping of markets into nested families by indication, label breadth and deadline
Subset-relationship checks with alerting on violations
Capital patient enough to hold both legs through a long regulatory timeline

name: Market Making / Liquidity Provision
description: Instead of betting on an outcome, you post buy and sell orders on both sides of a market and earn the small gap between them (the bid/ask spread) as other traders trade against you. You make money on the spread over many fills, like a shop earning markup on volume. The main risk is inventory: if you end up holding too much of one side, you can lose if the price runs against you, so a fair-value estimate and position limits keep you balanced.
requirements: Bot that continuously quotes and re-quotes around fair value
Inventory and position limits to cap directional exposure
A fair-value model to anchor quote midpoint

name: Scalping Narrow Spreads
description: Repeatedly capture tiny profits off the gap between bid and ask in high-volume markets, getting in and out constantly. There's almost no edge per trade; the money comes from doing it thousands of times with very low fees and fast execution, so volume and cost efficiency, not any single call, drive the profit.
requirements: Extremely low effective transaction cost (gas/fees)
Execution engine that can submit/cancel orders rapidly
Daily PnL attribution to confirm the edge is real after costs

name: Inventory-Aware Market Making
description: A market-making strategy that tilts your quotes based on the inventory you already hold, so the bot is more eager to sell when long and to buy when short. This nudges your position back toward neutral automatically (the Avellaneda-Stoikov approach) instead of piling up one-sided risk, letting you keep collecting the bid-ask spread while controlling exposure.
requirements: Real-time inventory tracker per market
Quote-skew model (e.g., Avellaneda-Stoikov style)
Risk dashboard with hard position kill-switch

name: Order-Book Imbalance Quote Skewing
description: This market-making strategy adjusts your buy and sell quotes based on which side of the order book is heavier. If there's little resting size opposing one side, you quote that side tighter and more aggressively; if a wall of orders is stacked against the other side, you back off and widen it. The edge is that on Polymarket's thin books, lopsided depth tends to predict which way price drifts next.
requirements: WSS CLOB order-book feed with full depth
Sub-second requote loop via CLOB REST/signed orders
Imbalance signal model calibrated per market
USDC inventory across both outcome tokens

name: Maker-Rebate Volume Farming
description: Polymarket pays liquidity rewards to traders who post resting orders near the best price in eligible high-volume markets. This strategy posts passive maker orders sized and placed to maximize that reward score (staying close to the best price and keeping orders up most of the time), rather than to profit from the spread itself. The edge is the subsidy: you aim to trade roughly break-even while the incentive program pays you.
requirements: Tracking of active liquidity-reward program markets/params
Uptime-monitored quoting bot near reward spread bands
Inventory auto-flattening to stay delta-neutral
Capital spread across rewarded books

name: Layered Iceberg Quoting
description: Instead of showing one big resting order, you split it into a ladder of small clips and quietly refill them as they fill, so only a little size is visible at the best price at any moment. This hides how much you really want to trade. The edge is that informed traders can't read your true depth, so you suffer fewer bad fills than if you displayed full size on a thin book.
requirements: Order ladder manager with auto-replenish on partial fills
Low-latency cancel/replace pipeline
Per-level size and spacing model
Fill-rate and toxicity telemetry

name: Toxic-Flow Detection & Quote Pull
description: As a market maker, you score the incoming orders hitting your quotes for how 'toxic' they are, meaning how often they're followed by a sharp move against you (using post-trade markouts, the aggressor's wallet history, and bursty patterns). When toxicity spikes, you pull or widen your quotes for a moment, then re-engage once the flow calms down. The edge is dodging informed or insider traders who would otherwise pick you off.
requirements: Per-fill markout (post-trade price) computation
On-chain aggressor wallet labeling/history DB
Real-time toxicity classifier with quote-pull trigger
Fast cancel infra

name: Catalyst-Window Spread Widening
description: Around scheduled events that can move a market suddenly (a poll release, a Fed inflation print, the final minutes of a game, an oracle resolution window), you automatically widen your quoted spread and shrink your size, then tighten back up once the moment passes. The edge is staying in the spread-capture business most of the time while sidestepping the predictable information shocks that would burn you.
requirements: Calendar of per-market catalyst timestamps
Volatility/spread schedule keyed to catalyst proximity
Automated spread/size scaling in quoting engine
Event-feed ingestion for ad-hoc catalysts

name: Latency-Aware Stale-Quote Cancellation
description: You constantly estimate the true price from faster-moving reference venues (crypto exchanges, sportsbooks, related markets) and cancel any of your resting quotes that has gone stale against that fair value before a taker can pick it off, then re-post around the updated price. The edge is minimizing how often you get run over during the brief delay it takes to cancel an order on Polygon.
requirements: Low-latency fair-value feed from leading reference venues
Stale-quote detector with cancel-on-drift trigger
Measured cancel round-trip latency budget
Cross-venue price normalization

name: Inventory-Skew Mean-Reversion Quoting
description: You quote evenly on both sides only when your position is flat. As you accumulate one outcome token, you tilt both your buy and sell quotes to encourage trades that shrink the position back toward neutral, even paying a little to do so, before resolution risk concentrates. The edge is capturing the spread while keeping a tight cap on directional exposure to a binary outcome.
requirements: Real-time position/inventory tracker per outcome token
Inventory-to-skew control function with hard caps
Two-sided quoting engine
Reservation-price model (Avellaneda-Stoikov analog)

name: Spread-Capture Re-Pegging on Wide Books
description: In markets that are chronically wide and have few competing market makers, you post just inside the existing spread to become the best bid or ask, then keep nudging one tick inside any new competitor. Because the spread stays wide, each round trip earns a meaningful margin. The edge is harvesting the illiquidity premium in neglected long-tail markets before other makers show up.
requirements: Scanner ranking markets by spread width vs maker competition
Auto-peg/undercut quoting with min-margin floor
Per-market fill and turnover monitoring
Small capital spread across many thin books

name: Liquidity-Mining Reward-Adjusted Quoting
description: Quote both buy and sell sides in markets covered by Polymarket's liquidity-provider reward program, placing orders to maximize your reward score (which weights tight spreads, depth, and uptime) so the subsidy income alone beats the cost of being picked off, even when your raw spread is roughly break-even. The edge is treating the reward formula itself as the profit source and shaping inventory to stay inside the reward-eligible bands.
requirements: Reverse-engineered LP reward scoring formula + eligible-market list
Quoting bot tracking reward bands and uptime
Capital across many rewarded books simultaneously
Adverse-selection vs subsidy PnL attribution model

name: LP Concentration & Reward-Decay Rotation
description: Move your provided liquidity from market to market to capture the most reward incentives (tokens paid for market-making), since each market's reward rate shrinks as more money piles in. You exit a pool the moment the extra reward no longer covers the risk of trading against better-informed flow. The edge is treating those mining rewards like a yield that's richest right when a market is freshly incentivized.
requirements: Real-time per-market reward-rate and TVL telemetry
Yield model netting emissions vs expected adverse selection
Automated multi-market LP add/remove with gas batching
Capital sized to move into freshly-incentivized listings fast

name: Two-Sided Spoof-Resistant Penny-Jump Quoting
description: On thin order books, watch when a rival market-maker parks one tick better than the best price, and step in front of them by the minimum increment, but only when real resting size sits behind that price rather than fake flicker that gets cancelled instantly. The edge is telling a genuine queue apart from spoofed bluffs by measuring how long orders actually live.
requirements: Full L2 book with per-order add/cancel timestamping
Cancel-rate / order-lifetime classifier per counterparty
Tick-by-tick re-quote engine with anti-self-cross guard
Inventory caps to bound directional fills from jumping

name: Halftime & Between-Period Repricing Lag
description: During a break in play there is no new information, but there is a wave of traders repositioning at once, and the book gets thin and jumpy. You quote both sides through the break around a fair value anchored to your win-probability model, collecting the spread from people who want out or in immediately. Because nothing can actually happen while the clock is stopped, inventory risk during the break itself is unusually low.
requirements: Model fair value that holds steady through stoppages rather than drifting with flow
Automated quoting with inventory caps and a hard flatten before play resumes
Knowledge of each sport's break timings so quoting starts and stops precisely

name: Cycle Quoting with Spot-Delta Hedge
description: Quoting both sides of an hourly up/down market leaves you holding directional risk whenever one side fills more than the other. Crypto is the one category where you can neutralise that instantly, because the underlying trades 24/7 on a dozen venues: you offset the inventory with a small spot or perp position and go back to earning the spread. The hedge ratio is the market's sensitivity to price, which rises sharply as the cycle nears its close.
requirements: Two-sided quoting bot with live inventory tracking per cycle
Funded spot or perp account for hedging, with the delta recomputed continuously
Model of how sensitivity to price grows into the settlement window

name: Pre-Game Quoting Against the Consensus Line
description: In the hours before a game the sportsbook consensus is a very stable fair value, which makes it an unusually safe anchor to quote around. You post both sides at a spread either side of the book-implied probability and collect from traders who want in or out immediately. The discipline is knowing exactly when to stop: lineup confirmations, injury news and the closing-line move are all scheduled or semi-scheduled events that make you the slow side.
requirements: Live consensus line from several books converted to a fair probability after vig
Automated quoting with inventory caps and per-game exposure limits
Hard pull rules tied to lineup release times and injury-wire hits

name: Between-Map Quoting in Best-of Series
description: The gap between maps in a best-of-three is a genuine pause with no play happening, but a burst of repositioning as everyone digests the result just posted. You quote both sides of the series market through that window around a fair value derived from the new score and each team's remaining map strength. Because nothing can happen while the players are on the break, inventory risk during the window itself is close to zero.
requirements: Series fair-value model that reprices instantly on each map result
Automated quoting that starts at map end and flattens before the next map begins
Per-map strength ratings so the fair value reflects what is still to be played

name: Model-Run Clock Quoting
description: Weather markets have an unusually predictable information schedule: nothing much changes between model runs, then a great deal changes at once when a new one lands. That makes the quoting posture obvious — earn the spread through the quiet stretch, then widen or pull entirely in the minutes around each 00z, 06z, 12z and 18z release. The mistake that kills weather market makers is leaving quotes up across a run boundary.
requirements: Model-release calendar with the actual availability times, not the nominal cycle hours
Automated widen-and-pull tied to those timestamps
Fair value that updates from the new run before quoting resumes

name: Data-Release Quote Ladder
description: Macro markets live on a public calendar: the number drops at 8:30am ET and everything else is waiting. That structure makes the quoting plan mechanical — earn the spread across the quiet days, step the spread wider as the release approaches, and go flat entirely for the print. The traders who lose money here are the ones still quoting tight at 8:29, filling everyone who is faster on the number.
requirements: Economic release calendar with exact publication times per series
Automated spread widening on a schedule, then full withdrawal before the print
Post-release fair-value update before quotes are allowed to resume

name: Earnings-Window Quoting with a Listed-Option Hedge
description: Company markets cluster around earnings, which is exactly when quoting is most dangerous and most profitable. Stocks are the one category where the inventory you accumulate can be hedged with an instrument that pays off on the identical event: a listed option struck at the same level. You quote the spread into the earnings run-up and offset the resulting exposure in the option chain, then flatten before the release itself.
requirements: Brokerage access to the listed option chain for each company you quote
Mapping from prediction-market exposure to the equivalent option position
Hard flatten rule before the earnings release, when the hedge gets expensive

name: Election-Night Quoting on the Reporting Curve
description: Election night is the highest-volume, widest-spread window political markets ever see, and most of the flow is emotional rather than informed. A market maker with an expected-vote model has a fair value nobody else in the book has, and can quote both sides through the swings that the running total produces. The risk is a genuine call or a reporting surprise, so quoting must stop the moment a race is called or the reporting pattern breaks from the model.
requirements: Live expected-vote model producing a fair value from partial county returns
Two-sided quoting with tight inventory caps and rapid re-pegging
Automatic withdrawal on a race call or when reporting diverges from the model

name: Headline-Risk Quoting with a Wire Kill Switch
description: Geopolitical markets are the most dangerous place to quote — nothing happens for weeks and then a single wire headline moves a market thirty points. The only viable posture is a wide spread that pays for that risk, small size, and an automated kill switch wired directly to the news feeds so quotes are pulled within milliseconds of any relevant story. You are being paid for providing liquidity in a market where the tail is genuinely fat.
requirements: Wire and agency feed monitoring with keyword triggers per market you quote
Automatic quote cancellation on any trigger, before human assessment
Spread and size calibrated to historical headline gap moves, not average volatility

name: Speech-Window Quoting
description: A mention market has a completely known risk schedule: nothing can resolve it until the speech starts, and then it can resolve in a single second. That makes the quoting posture unusually clean — quote both sides through the days beforehand, when the only movement is speculation, and go entirely flat the moment the audio begins. Quoting live during a speech means being picked off by whoever has the faster feed, which is a race you will not win.
requirements: Appearance calendar with confirmed start times for every market you quote
Fair value anchored to a base-rate model rather than to recent order flow
Automated flatten at speech start, with no manual override

name: Weekend Box-Office Reporting-Cycle Quoting
description: Box-office markets follow a rigid weekly rhythm: Thursday previews, Friday actuals late that night, studio estimates Sunday morning, actuals Monday. Between those drops nothing changes, and at each one everything does. You quote both sides through the dead stretches and pull ahead of every scheduled number, then re-anchor fair value on the new figure. The whole strategy is knowing the reporting calendar better than the people you are quoting to.
requirements: Box-office reporting calendar with the actual publication times for each figure
Weekend-multiplier model so fair value updates correctly on each partial number
Automated pull-and-requote around every scheduled release

name: Rumor-Window Quoting on Launch Markets
description: Product-launch markets spend most of their life in a rumor phase with no resolvable information, which is ideal quoting territory: flow is steady, the fair value barely moves, and the participants are speculating rather than informed. The risk is concentrated in known windows — keynote events, scheduled announcements, embargo lifts. You earn the spread through the rumor stretch and stand fully aside for every dated event on the calendar.
requirements: Event calendar covering keynotes, developer conferences and known announcement dates
Fair value anchored to a release-cadence hazard model rather than to rumor volume
Automated withdrawal ahead of every scheduled event and embargo lift

name: Decision-Date Quoting Around a Known Catalyst
description: A regulatory decision market has a published target date, which splits its life cleanly into a long quiet stretch and one violent moment. That is the ideal shape for a market maker: quote a moderate spread for months while the only flow is positioning, then go completely flat well before the decision window opens. The mistake is assuming the agency will use the whole clock — decisions and rejection letters both arrive early sometimes.
requirements: Decision-date calendar with the historical distribution of early actions per agency
Fair value from phase- and pathway-specific approval base rates
Flatten rule that starts well before the target date, not on it

name: News-Event Reaction Trading
description: You wire up fast news feeds (wire services, X) and pre-stage orders so that the instant a market-moving story breaks, your trade fires before most humans have even read the headline. The edge is pure speed: prediction-market prices take seconds to minutes to catch up to fresh news, and you capture that lag. A classifier maps each headline to the specific market it affects so the right order goes out automatically.
requirements: Low-latency news API (Reuters, AP, benzinga, X firehose, etc.)
Keyword/LLM classifier mapping stories to specific markets
Pre-approved order templates with tight execution SLAs

name: Social Sentiment Signal
description: You collect the mood of social platforms (X, Reddit, Truth Social, Telegram) around topics tied to specific markets, score whether the chatter is turning bullish or bearish, and trade when that sentiment clearly disagrees with the current market price. The bet is that a real shift in public opinion shows up in posts before it shows up fully in the price. Spam and bot filtering matter a lot, since fake activity can fake out the signal.
requirements: Streaming social data pipeline with dedupe and spam filters
Sentiment model (LLM or fine-tuned classifier) tuned per topic
Backtested threshold for when to act on a sentiment shift

name: Whale Wallet Tracking
description: Every Polymarket trade is recorded on-chain, so you can watch the wallets of large traders who have made money over time. When one of these proven wallets opens a position, you copy it (or get in just ahead). The edge is borrowing the research and conviction of sharp money. The danger is being their exit liquidity, so you need rules to avoid buying right as a whale is about to sell out of a position.
requirements: On-chain indexer for Polymarket contract activity (Polygon)
Curated list of wallets with positive historical PnL
Risk rules so you aren't the exit liquidity for a reversal

name: Bot Front-Running Detection
description: Watch the order book for other bots that trade mechanically (for example, one that always places a buy a fixed amount below the best offer) and place your own order just ahead of where that bot will predictably trade next. You profit from the price pressure the other bot creates when it fills, because you are positioned in front of its move.
requirements: Order-book replay data and pattern-mining tools
Very low-latency execution to beat the target bot
Compliance check that the strategy respects platform ToS

name: Google Trends / Search-Volume Signals
description: Use public search-interest data (Google Trends, pytrends) as an early warning signal for markets driven by public attention, such as a candidate, a product launch, or a viral event. The edge is timing: a sharp spike in searches often precedes the Polymarket price move, so you position before the crowd catches up, while filtering out unrelated search noise.
requirements: Google Trends API / pytrends scraping with rate limits
Backtest showing trend spikes precede Polymarket moves
Noise filter to avoid reacting to unrelated search surges

name: Copy-Trading High-Performers
description: Rank Polymarket wallets by their risk-adjusted past profits (return per unit of risk taken), then automatically mirror a weighted basket of the top performers' new trades, with caps so no single wallet dominates your book. You're piggybacking on traders who have a proven edge, and you unwind when a leader reverses.
requirements: Leaderboard computed from on-chain Polymarket trade history
Position-mirroring bot with per-wallet size limits
Rebalancing and unwind logic when a leader reverses

name: Contrarian Crowd-Fade
description: When a market jumps sharply on social-media hype rather than real news, bet against the move and wait for the price to drift back once the excitement fades. The edge comes from detecting the divergence between chatter volume and actual news flow, then fading the overreaction, with a time-stop in case you're wrong.
requirements: Hype detection (mention-volume vs. news-volume divergence)
Price-move vs. news-flow comparison
Time-stop in case the contrarian view is wrong

name: Poll-Drop Reaction Bot
description: When a major pollster drops a new survey, your bot reads it instantly and trades on how Polymarket usually over- or under-reacts to that specific pollster. The edge is your per-pollster model: you know the market tends to overshoot certain houses and underweight others, so you fire orders before the price finds its true level, with a kill-switch for unknown pollsters.
requirements: Monitoring of pollster release schedules and feeds
Per-pollster reaction model (historic over/undershoot)
Kill-switch for surprise non-canonical pollsters

name: Flight-Tracking OSINT for Geopolitical Markets
description: You watch live aircraft-tracking feeds (ADS-B Exchange, OpenSky) for unusual movements of government, military, or diplomatic planes, like a leader's jet suddenly diverting or transport aircraft massing, and trade Polymarket geopolitical and conflict markets before the news reports it. The edge is that physical-world signals can lead the news wire by minutes to hours.
requirements: ADS-B Exchange/OpenSky API + tail-number watchlist (gov/military registries)
Pattern-detection code flagging anomalous routes/divergences
Mapping of aircraft events to specific open Polymarket conflict/diplomacy markets
Low-latency CLOB execution to hit liquidity before repricing

name: Maritime AIS Shipping Signal
description: Watch live ship-location data (AIS, the GPS-style transponder every large vessel broadcasts) to spot tankers going dark, ports jamming up, or navy movements at chokepoints like Hormuz and Suez, then bet on the related commodity, sanctions, or conflict markets. The edge: the physical movement of ships happens days before officials confirm it or news narratives form, so you trade the fact before the story.
requirements: AIS feed (MarineTraffic/Spire/Global Fishing Watch) with vessel-class tagging
Dark-ship and chokepoint-congestion detection model
Linkage of vessel events to sanctions/commodity/conflict markets
Capital to hold positions through multi-day physical-event windows

name: Betting-Exchange Volume & Vig Leakage
description: Sharp betting exchanges like Betfair and Smarkets trade huge volume and price events faster and more accurately than Polymarket. You strip out their built-in margin (the 'vig') to get their true implied probability, then trade Polymarket whenever its price still lags the exchange's line on the same event. The edge is pure information leakage: the deeper, faster market moves first and Polymarket's order book catches up slowly.
requirements: Betfair/Smarkets API for live odds + matched volume
Vig-removal and event-matching engine across venue taxonomies
Latency-aware execution to capture lag before convergence
Risk limits for venue-specific resolution-criteria mismatches

name: Telegram/Discord Insider-Channel Mining
description: Use automated text-monitoring (NLP) to watch high-signal Telegram and Discord channels — crypto-launch insiders, political operatives, sports injury leakers, war-reporting groups — and trade the matching Polymarket before the news reaches Twitter or mainstream outlets. The edge is that these niche communities reliably break market-moving information first, and you act in the gap before it spreads.
requirements: Telegram MTProto + Discord gateway scrapers across curated channel set
LLM/NLP classifier scoring messages for actionable, market-relevant claims
Source-reliability weighting and false-rumor filtering
Fast execution + position caps per unverified-rumor trade

name: GDELT Global-Event Stream Trading
description: GDELT is a free feed that machine-reads global news every 15 minutes and scores the tone and type of each event (conflict, protest, coup, instability). You watch for sudden spikes in negative coverage about a country or actor and buy the related geopolitical market before the narrative consolidates. The edge is that automated worldwide news monitoring surfaces escalations faster than any human watching headlines.
requirements: GDELT 2.0 GKG/Events 15-min feed ingestion + storage
Country/actor tone & Goldstein-scale anomaly model
Mapping of event-code spikes to open instability/conflict markets
Backtested thresholds to suppress noise-driven false signals

name: Polymarket Comment-Section Sentiment Edge
description: Scrape Polymarket's own per-market comment threads and trader-activity feed, then run text analysis to detect when informed holders shift conviction, when a coordinated narrative is being pushed, or when holders capitulate — signals that tend to precede the price move inside that same market. The edge is that this native sentiment surface is unique to the platform and almost nobody mines it systematically.
requirements: Polymarket comment + activity API/scraper with per-market history
Sentiment + conviction-scoring model tuned on resolved-market outcomes
Linkage of commenter wallet history to credibility weighting
Execution logic triggered on sentiment-vs-price divergence

name: Cross-Market Information Leakage Mapping
description: Map out Polymarket markets that are logically linked (e.g. 'wins the primary' should move 'wins the general'), and when a leading market reprices on news, trade the related lagging market before arbitrage bots equalize the implied conditional probability. The edge is exploiting how slowly information travels across the platform's own web of connected markets.
requirements: Market-dependency graph + conditional-probability linkage model
Real-time price feed across all related markets
Lead-lag detection identifying which market moves first
Low-latency execution to capture the lagging leg

name: Prediction-Market Comment Bot-Swarm Detection
description: Detect coordinated influence campaigns — synchronized posting, clusters of bot accounts, planted narratives across Telegram, X, and Polymarket comments — that artificially push a market in one direction, then bet against the move, since these inorganic spikes tend to reverse once the campaign ends. The edge is telling fake, manufactured sentiment apart from real information and fading it.
requirements: Multi-platform social scraping with account-graph clustering
Coordination/bot-detection model (timing, content similarity, account age)
Historical mapping of detected campaigns to post-campaign reversion
Risk controls sizing against genuinely-informed minority signals

name: Economic-Data Nowcast from Alt Indicators
description: Combine fast-updating alternative data — Truflation, credit-card spending panels, gasoline and electricity demand, job-posting indices, freight rates — to build your own early estimate ('nowcast') of upcoming CPI, jobs, GDP, or rate-decision numbers before the official government release. The edge is that your private forecast can beat the consensus the market has already baked into its price.
requirements: Alt-data feeds (Truflation, ADP-adjacent, jobs/freight indices)
Nowcasting regression/ensemble mapping indicators to official prints
Historical alignment of nowcast error vs market-implied estimates
Capital + risk management for surprise-direction macro positions

name: Superforecaster Ensemble Disagreement Engine
description: Run a panel of AI forecasting bots over every open market, each given different prompts, source material, and personas, then blend their probability estimates into one number weighted by how accurate each bot has been in the past. You bet when that blended forecast disagrees with the market's price by more than normal noise. The edge is that superforecaster-style averaging beats the thin, lightly-traded crowd on under-followed Polymarket questions.
requirements: LLM API budget for multi-agent panels per market
Calibration dataset of resolved markets to weight agent skill
Gamma/CLOB feed for live mids + market metadata
Brier-score backtest harness for agent selection

name: Retrieval-Augmented Cross-Market Coherence Audit
description: A retrieval system (an AI that looks up and cites the actual market rules) builds a map of how markets logically relate: which ones are subsets, supersets, or can't both be true. An AI then checks whether their combined prices break the laws of probability, like P(A and B) priced higher than P(A) alone. You buy the underpriced leg and sell the overpriced one to capture the inconsistency.
requirements: Embedding index over all market rule text
LLM logic-relation extractor (implication/exclusion)
Live multi-leg pricing + basket execution
Constraint-solver to size coherence trades

name: Multi-Agent Debate Convergence Signal
description: For each market, stage a structured AI debate: one agent argues Yes, one argues No, and a judge agent updates its estimate over several rounds. The signal is how fast and how firmly the judge settles toward one side. Markets where the debate converges strongly against the current price get bigger bets; wishy-washy debates are skipped. The edge is that disciplined back-and-forth reasoning exposes prices that are falsely confident.
requirements: Orchestration for multi-round LLM debate per market
Judge-agent calibration against resolved outcomes
Confidence-to-size mapping + risk overlay
Compute budget for repeated debate runs

name: RAG Market-Scanner for Cold New Listings
description: A retrieval-augmented agent (an AI that looks up relevant facts on demand) watches for brand-new market listings and, within minutes, gathers the priors that matter, base rates, expert sources, and similar markets that already resolved, to price the new market before real trading volume shows up. The edge is being the first informed bettor on a fresh contract whose opening price was set by uninformed guessing.
requirements: Real-time new-market listing detector
RAG index of base rates + analogous historical markets
Fast LLM pricing + initial position sizing
Inventory/risk limits for illiquid fresh markets

name: LLM Sentiment-vs-Fundamentals Divergence Map
description: Two AI pipelines score each market in parallel: one reads social and narrative buzz, the other digs up hard facts from trusted sources. When hype has dragged the price far away from the fundamentals estimate, you bet against the hype. The edge is isolating the boring fundamentals signal that loud crowd over-reaction tends to drown out.
requirements: Social/feed ingestion + sentiment-scoring agent
Fundamentals-retrieval agent with source whitelist
Divergence threshold calibrated on resolved markets
Position + risk engine to fade overextended moves

name: FX-Implied Drift on USD-Denominated Macro Markets
description: Convert live signals from the deep traditional markets, FX rates, rate futures, and inflation swaps, into implied probabilities for dollar-based macro questions like rate cuts, inflation prints, and currency pegs, then trade the gap when Polymarket is slow to follow the rates complex. The edge is importing the fast, well-informed bond and FX markets' view into a slower prediction venue.
requirements: Real-time FX, OIS/rate-futures and inflation-swap data feed
Conversion model from market-implied rates to event probabilities
Latency budget to act before macro arbs reprice the contract
Sizing aware of basis risk between proxy and exact resolution

name: Counterparty Smart-Money Clustering & Fade/Follow
description: Group on-chain Polymarket traders into clusters by how much real edge they've shown and how well they time entries, then follow the consistently profitable group and bet against the consistently losing group whenever either places a fresh, oversized position. The edge is attributing skill at the wallet level using the whole trade graph, rather than blindly copying one famous whale.
requirements: Full historical fills indexed by wallet with realized-PnL labels
Clustering/skill-scoring model with out-of-sample validation
Real-time new-position detection per tracked cohort
Position sizing decorrelated across overlapping cohort signals

name: Perp Funding-Rate Skew on Hourly Up/Down Cycles
description: Perpetual futures charge a small recurring payment called funding from whichever side of the trade is crowded — when funding turns sharply positive, leveraged buyers are paying to stay long, and vice versa. That number is a live census of positioning that Polymarket's short-dated up/down cycles do not price directly. You read funding and open interest across the big perp venues at the start of each cycle and lean against extreme crowding, because over-levered books tend to get flushed inside the hour.
requirements: Funding-rate and open-interest feeds from 2+ perp venues (Binance, Bybit, Hyperliquid)
Per-cycle mapping from funding extremes to a probability tilt, backtested on past cycles
Position limits per cycle so a persistent funding regime doesn't compound one-way risk

name: Depth-Wall Fade Around Round-Number Strikes
description: Big resting orders cluster at round numbers like $100,000, and those walls act as speed bumps: price often stalls or reverses when it hits one. Polymarket strike markets sitting just beyond a wall are frequently priced as if the level does not exist. You monitor aggregate order-book depth on the major spot venues, identify the walls nearest a market's strike, and fade the markets that ignore them. The signal decays fast, because walls get pulled the moment they are tested.
requirements: Aggregated level-2 depth across the top spot venues, refreshed continuously
Wall-detection logic that distinguishes real resting size from spoofed, quickly-pulled orders
Rapid exit when the wall is consumed rather than defended

name: Spot-ETF Net-Flow Print Reaction
description: Spot crypto ETFs publish daily creation and redemption totals after the US close, and those flows are a clean read on institutional demand that shows up on a fixed schedule. Sustained inflows have historically preceded firmer prices over the following days, and a run of large outflows the opposite. You ingest each issuer's daily file the moment it posts and take positions in the multi-day and end-of-month crypto markets before the number gets absorbed into the narrative the next morning.
requirements: Automated pull of per-issuer daily flow disclosures at their publication times
Rolling flow-vs-return study to size the tilt honestly rather than by feel
Awareness of month-end and quarter-end rebalancing distortions

name: Exchange Reserve & Netflow Divergence
description: Coins moving onto exchanges are usually being prepared for sale; coins moving off are usually going into storage. Aggregated exchange balances therefore act as a slow-moving supply gauge you can read directly from the chain. When reserves are draining hard while the market prices continue to lean bearish, that disagreement is the trade. It works best on multi-day and monthly markets, since the signal is measured in days, not minutes.
requirements: On-chain analytics feed for exchange wallet clustering and net flows
Filters for internal transfers and custody migrations, which fake out raw balances
Multi-day holding horizon matched to how slowly the signal actually moves

name: Injury-Report Wire Race
description: A star player being ruled out is worth several percentage points of win probability, and that news breaks on a small number of beat-reporter accounts minutes before it reaches the official injury report. You monitor those specific accounts plus league injury APIs, map each player to a pre-computed impact number, and fire orders on the affected game markets the moment a status changes. This is a pure speed play: the whole edge lives in the two-to-ten-minute window before the market absorbs it.
requirements: Streaming monitor on league injury endpoints plus a curated list of beat reporters
Pre-computed per-player win-probability impact so no thinking happens at trade time
Automated order templates with strict latency budgets and a false-report kill switch

name: Starting-Lineup & Goalie-Confirmation Snap
description: In soccer, hockey and baseball, the confirmed lineup drops at a predictable time before first whistle — an hour out in the Premier League, on the morning skate in the NHL — and it can swing a match materially, particularly the starting goaltender or pitcher. Until that moment, the market prices an average across plausible lineups. You pre-model each likely lineup's win probability so that when the sheet posts, you already know the new fair price and can act inside seconds.
requirements: Lineup and probable-starter feeds with per-league release-time schedules
Pre-built win-probability deltas for each plausible lineup or starter permutation
Execution ready to fire in the narrow window right after the announcement

name: Transfer-Window & Trade-Deadline Rumor Tiering
description: Player-movement markets are dominated by rumor, and not all rumors are equal — a handful of reporters have documented hit rates near 90% while aggregator accounts are barely better than noise. You score every claim by the historical reliability of its source, treat 'here we go'-class reporting as near-confirmation, and fade markets that spike on low-tier sourcing. The edge is being calibrated about journalists rather than about players.
requirements: Scored reliability table per reporter, maintained from past resolved rumors
Real-time monitoring of the tier-one accounts with instant classification
Rules for handling club-side denials, which are frequently meaningless

name: Roster-Change, Stand-In & Visa-Denial Watch
description: Esports rosters change constantly, and a team fielding a stand-in — because of illness, a benching or a denied travel visa — is materially weaker in a way that often is not priced until the match starts. These announcements appear on team social accounts and tournament admin channels, not on any structured feed. You monitor those channels directly, quantify each player's individual contribution, and act on lineup news within minutes.
requirements: Monitoring of team, player and tournament-admin social channels across regions
Per-player impact ratings so a stand-in can be priced immediately
Handling for late roster confirmations, which sometimes land minutes before the map starts

name: Station-Level Observation Nowcast
description: Daily-high temperature markets resolve on a specific official station, and by early afternoon that station has already reported most of what will decide the outcome. If the observed temperature is 93°F at 2pm with three hours of heating left, the question is nearly settled while the market is still pricing the morning forecast. You poll the resolving station's observations directly and trade the residual uncertainty rather than the forecast.
requirements: Direct polling of the exact resolving station (ASOS/METAR) at its reporting cadence
Diurnal heating curve model to project the remaining move to the daily peak
Verification that the market resolves on that station and not a regional average

name: Model-Run Cadence Repricing
description: Global weather models publish on a fixed schedule — 00z, 06z, 12z and 18z — and output becomes available at predictable minutes past those hours. Weather markets reprice in a burst after each run lands. If your pipeline parses the new run before manual traders have read the graphics, you get a short window at the old price. This is scheduled, repeatable, and available four times a day, every day.
requirements: Automated download and parse of raw model output within minutes of each run's release
Threshold-extraction code that turns raw fields into per-market probabilities immediately
Order staging so trades fire during the repricing window rather than after it

name: FOMC Statement-Diff & Dot-Plot Trading
description: The Fed's policy statement changes only a few words between meetings, and those words are chosen deliberately — dropping 'patient' or adding 'some further' is the actual message. You run an automated diff against the previous statement the instant it posts, score the changes on a hawkish-to-dovish scale calibrated on past reactions, and trade the follow-on markets about future meetings before the press conference even begins.
requirements: Statement scrape at release with an automated word-level diff against the prior version
Scoring model calibrated on historical statement changes and subsequent market moves
Separate handling for the quarterly projections, where the dot plot dominates the text

name: Central-Bank Speaker Calendar Drift
description: Between policy meetings, rate expectations get moved by scheduled speeches from voting members, and those appearances are published weeks ahead. Individual officials have consistent, measurable leanings, so a week loaded with hawkish speakers tends to drift expectations one way regardless of content. You build a speaker-weighted calendar, position ahead of clusters, and monitor the wires during each appearance for the specific phrases that historically moved pricing.
requirements: Speaker calendar with a hawkish-dovish score per official based on their voting history
Live transcript or wire monitoring during each scheduled appearance
Position sizing that respects how quickly individual speech effects decay

name: Guidance-Language Diff Trading
description: Companies reuse boilerplate quarter after quarter, so the sentences that change in a 10-Q, 8-K or earnings release are the ones carrying information — a removed risk factor, a softened outlook verb, a new litigation disclosure. You diff each filing against the prior period automatically at the moment it hits EDGAR and trade the company-outcome markets before anyone finishes reading the document. The filings arrive on a schedule, so this is repeatable rather than opportunistic.
requirements: EDGAR real-time filing monitor with automated section-level diffing
Classifier scoring which changes historically preceded material moves
Fast execution, since filings are parsed by many machines simultaneously

name: Short-Interest & Squeeze Setup Detection
description: A squeeze needs specific ingredients: high short interest relative to float, expensive borrow, low available lending inventory, and a catalyst. All four are observable. Markets asking whether a stock doubles or hits a big round number in a short window are essentially squeeze markets, and they get priced on chatter. You screen the mechanical conditions and only take the side when the plumbing supports it, which is far less often than social media suggests.
requirements: Short interest, borrow-fee and lending-availability data updated regularly
Float and retail-flow measures to gauge how tight the setup really is
Strict risk limits, since squeeze outcomes are extremely fat-tailed in both directions

name: Executive-Departure & Insider-Filing Signal
description: CEO exits are announced in an 8-K, but the tell often comes earlier: a cluster of Form 4 insider sales, a board-committee change, a quietly removed executive bio page. Markets asking whether a named executive leaves by a date are priced on speculation. You monitor the filing stream and corporate web pages for those precursors and take positions before the announcement makes it unanimous.
requirements: Form 4 and 8-K monitoring with per-company insider baselines to spot unusual clusters
Change-detection on leadership pages and board committee rosters
Base rates for executive tenure by sector to anchor the prior probability

name: Debate-Night Instant-Reaction Trading
description: Debate markets move violently in real time on moments that usually do not change the race, then partially revert once instant polls and focus-group results land an hour or two later. The historical record is clear that debate effects on actual vote share are small and short-lived. You fade the largest in-debate swings and take the other side of markets that reprice as though the race fundamentally changed, using post-debate polling as your exit signal.
requirements: Live transcript or caption feed plus real-time market monitoring during the debate
Historical study of debate-night moves versus eventual polling shifts
Fast access to instant polls and focus-group results for the exit decision

name: Campaign-Finance Viability Signal
description: Quarterly FEC filings reveal cash on hand, burn rate and the small-donor base — the three numbers that determine whether a campaign can still advertise in the states that matter. A candidate with two months of runway is not a serious contender no matter how the polling reads. You parse the filings the day they post and trade nomination, primary and drop-out markets before the reporting cycle catches up.
requirements: Automated FEC filing ingestion on each quarterly and pre-primary deadline
Burn-rate and runway modeling, including outside-group spending on the candidate's behalf
Ad-buy tracking as a real-time complement between filing deadlines

name: Ceasefire & Communiqué Wire Race
description: Ceasefires, hostage deals and peace frameworks are announced through a small, predictable set of channels: state news agencies, foreign-ministry accounts, and mediator statements — often in the local language hours before the English wires pick it up. You monitor those primary sources with automatic translation and trade the moment an authoritative announcement lands. The edge is monolingual traders waiting for an English headline.
requirements: Direct monitoring of state agencies and ministry accounts in the relevant languages
Machine translation with a confidence gate to avoid trading on a bad rendering
Source-authority tiering, since rumor and official confirmation resolve very differently

name: Sanctions-List Update Monitor
description: Sanctions designations are published as structured files by Treasury's OFAC and the EU's equivalent, usually with no advance warning, and markets about specific individuals, entities or countries resolve directly off those lists. You poll the official data files rather than waiting for coverage, diff each update against the last, and trade within seconds of a designation appearing. It is the rare geopolitical market with a machine-readable resolution source.
requirements: Polling of the OFAC SDN file and EU consolidated list with automated diffing
Entity name-matching that survives transliteration and alias variation
Alerting and order staging tied directly to the diff output

name: Trade-Flow & Customs-Data Signal
description: Tariff, embargo and export-control markets resolve on policy announcements, but the pressure that produces them shows up first in customs data, port throughput and shipping manifests. A sharp change in a bilateral flow — a collapse in chip exports, a surge in oil moving on shadow-fleet tankers — precedes the formal policy response by weeks. You track the flows and position ahead of the announcement.
requirements: Customs and bilateral trade statistics plus port-call and vessel-tracking data
Commodity-specific baselines so a seasonal swing isn't mistaken for a policy signal
Mapping from observed flow anomalies to the specific policy markets they bear on

name: Live-Transcript Word-Count Race
description: Mention markets ask whether a specific person says a specific word during a speech, hearing or broadcast, and they resolve on the transcript. Automated speech-to-text on the live audio stream gives you the count seconds before human viewers register it and well before the official transcript posts. You run recognition on the feed, match against the market's exact target phrase, and fire immediately on a confirmed hit.
requirements: Real-time speech-to-text on the live audio or video stream
Exact phrase-matching that respects the market's stated definition, including variants
Confidence thresholds so a mis-transcription doesn't trigger a bad fill

name: Critic-Score Threshold Model
description: Aggregate critic scores start with a small number of festival or embargo-lift reviews and converge as the full set lands, and the early sample is a biased but informative predictor of the final number. Markets asking whether a film clears a score threshold reprice violently on the first few reviews. You model the convergence from partial samples, including which outlets historically score above or below the eventual average, and fade the overreaction.
requirements: Review-by-review ingestion with per-outlet historical scoring bias
Convergence model estimating the final aggregate from a partial sample
Embargo-calendar tracking so you know when the sample will jump

name: Celebrity-Event Rumor Tiering
description: Personal-life markets — engagements, splits, births, public appearances — run on tabloid reporting of wildly varying reliability, from outlets with strong confirmation records to ones that publish speculation as fact. You maintain accuracy scores per outlet from previously resolved stories and trade only when a tier-one source reports, fading the spikes driven by aggregators. It is source calibration applied to the least rigorous corner of the market.
requirements: Outlet reliability scoring built from past resolved rumor markets
Real-time monitoring of the highest-tier outlets and official representative statements
Rules for handling non-denials and representative 'no comment' responses

name: Leaderboard-Submission Watch
description: Public model leaderboards frequently expose anonymous or codenamed entries during evaluation, days before an official announcement, and their scores are visible to anyone polling the API. A mysterious high-scoring entrant is a strong tell about both who is shipping and how good it is. You poll the leaderboards continuously, diff the entrant list, and trade benchmark and release markets on the appearance of an unexplained new row.
requirements: Continuous polling of the major leaderboards and evaluation APIs with entrant diffing
Attribution heuristics linking codenames to labs from response style and metadata
Careful reading of which benchmark and version each market resolves on

name: Chip-Supply & Fab-Capacity Signal
description: Hardware-dependent milestones — data-center buildouts, device launches, production targets — are gated by semiconductor supply, and that supply is visible in advance through foundry utilization disclosures, packaging capacity reports, export-control changes and lead-time surveys. When capacity is constrained, ambitious timelines slip. You track the supply chain and fade the markets pricing a launch date the physical inputs cannot support.
requirements: Foundry and packaging capacity reporting plus component lead-time data
Export-control and trade-restriction monitoring for the relevant categories
Mapping from supply constraints to the specific product and milestone markets affected

name: Repository-Activity Leading Indicator
description: Open-source projects broadcast their roadmap through their commit history: release branches get cut, version strings get bumped, changelogs get staged, and dependency pins move — all publicly, often weeks before a release announcement. You watch the repositories tied to each open market and treat a cut release branch as a strong, dated signal. For companies that develop in the open, this is the closest thing to reading the internal schedule.
requirements: Repository monitoring for branch creation, tags, version bumps and changelog staging
Historical mapping from each project's branch-cut to actual release lag
Filtering for abandoned branches and pre-release tags that never ship

name: Bootcamp & Scrim-Result Intelligence
description: Teams practise against each other in private scrims before every major event, and those results leak constantly — through player streams left running, coach and analyst chatter, and community trackers that log them. Scrim form is a genuinely predictive read on who has solved the current patch, and it is invisible to anyone pricing off public match history. You collect the leaks, weight them by source, and trade tournament markets before the first official game.
requirements: Monitoring of player streams, community scrim trackers and staff social accounts
Source scoring, since scrim results are noisy and teams deliberately experiment
Fast decay on the signal, because scrim form goes stale within a patch cycle

name: Radar Nowcast for Same-Day Precipitation
