description: For a market asking whether it rains in a city today, the highest-value data is not a forecast model at all — it is the radar mosaic showing where the precipitation is right now and which way it is moving. Extrapolating current echoes forward one to three hours beats any model at that range. You ingest the radar feed, project cell motion over the resolving station, and trade the same-day markets on physical observation.
requirements: Radar mosaic ingestion with cell-tracking and motion extrapolation
Geofence on the exact resolving station rather than the metro area
Short holding horizon, since nowcast skill collapses past a few hours

name: Regional Fed Survey Nowcast
description: The regional Federal Reserve banks publish manufacturing and services surveys — Empire State, Philadelphia, Richmond, Dallas — throughout the month, and together they lead the national ISM figure that markets actually trade. Each one is a free, scheduled, partial preview of a number that moves prices when it lands weeks later. You build a weighted composite from the regionals as they arrive and trade the national threshold markets before the headline print.
requirements: Automated ingestion of each regional survey on its own release schedule
Regression mapping the regional composite onto the national index it predicts
Weighting that reflects each region's historical predictive power, not its size

name: Card-Spend & Foot-Traffic Panel Signal
description: Consumer companies are measurable before they report: anonymised card-transaction panels, mobile-location foot traffic and app-download counts track quarterly revenue with a lag of days rather than months. These panels are commercially available and are used heavily by funds, but almost never by prediction-market traders. You build the quarterly estimate from the panel and trade the revenue and beat markets in the weeks before the print.
requirements: Subscription to a card-spend or foot-traffic panel with company-level coverage
Calibration of panel coverage against reported revenue over past quarters
Awareness of coverage bias — panels skew by demographic and geography

name: Ad-Buy & Media-Reservation Tracking
description: Campaigns reserve television airtime weeks ahead, and those reservations are filed publicly with the FCC station by station. Where a campaign is spending — and, more tellingly, where it has cancelled reservations — is a direct read on its own internal polling, which is far better than any public poll. You track the filings and trade the race markets on what the campaigns believe about themselves rather than on what they say.
requirements: Automated retrieval of FCC political-file filings across the relevant media markets
Normalisation of buys into per-voter spending by district or state
Alerting on cancellations and late additions, which carry the most information

name: Scripted-vs-Q&A Segment Split
description: The same speaker uses very different vocabulary in a scripted segment than in unscripted question time — earnings calls are the clearest case, where the prepared statement is lawyered and the analyst Q&A is loose. A word that will never appear in the script frequently appears in the answers. You model the two segments separately, and during a live event you reprice sharply at the moment the format switches.
requirements: Segment-tagged transcript corpus separating prepared remarks from open questions
Per-segment word frequency rates for each speaker
Live detection of the transition point during the event itself

name: Presale & Venue On-Sale Signal
description: Before a tour is announced, arenas quietly place holds on dates, ticketing systems stage event pages, and presale codes circulate — all visible days ahead of the official announcement. The same is true of festival lineups, which leak through vendor and staging permits. You monitor venue calendars and ticketing infrastructure and trade announcement markets on the operational trail rather than the press release.
requirements: Monitoring of venue calendars, ticketing staging pages and presale code channels
Cross-referencing of holds across cities to distinguish a tour from a one-off
Source scoring, since holds are frequently placed and then released

name: Hiring & Job-Posting Direction Signal
description: Companies advertise their roadmap in their job postings long before they announce anything: a sudden cluster of hardware roles, a team being staffed in a new city, infrastructure engineers hired for a named capability. Postings are public, timestamped and structured. You track the postings for the companies behind your open markets and treat a hiring cluster as a leading indicator of what ships, and roughly when.
requirements: Automated collection of career-page postings with historical diffing per company
Classification of roles into product and capability areas
Lag model from hiring cluster to shipped product, fitted on past cycles

name: Inspection & Regulatory-Communication Watch
description: Regulatory outcomes are foreshadowed in paperwork that publishes before any decision: manufacturing inspection classifications, facility citations, advisory committee briefing documents posted days ahead of the meeting, and meeting agendas that reveal which questions the panel will actually be asked. An unresolved manufacturing citation has sunk approvals whose clinical data was fine. You monitor those documents and trade the approval markets on process evidence.
requirements: Monitoring of inspection databases, citation letters and advisory committee document postings
Facility-to-product mapping so a citation is linked to the right application
Base rates for how often each finding type delays or blocks a decision

name: Polling Aggregator Edge (Elections)
description: You build your own polling average for an election, adjusting each poll for known pollster bias ('house effects'), how recent it is, and sample size, to get a cleaner probability than any single poll. You then trade whenever the Polymarket price drifts away from your model's number. The edge is having a sharper, faster-updating estimate of the race than the crowd, and acting each time a new poll moves your average but the market hasn't caught up.
requirements: Ongoing ingestion of pollster-level data (538-style)
Model for house effects, trend line, and uncertainty
Rules for updating positions after each new poll drop

name: Base Rate Exploitation
description: A base rate is how often something happens historically, ignoring the current hype. This strategy finds markets where the crowd's price clearly ignores those long-run odds (for example, incumbents win reelection most of the time, no-hitters are rare) and bets the side that history favors. You won't win every trade, but across many markets where the crowd is far off the historical rate, the math works out. Discipline to ride out unlucky individual outcomes is essential.
requirements: Database of relevant historical base rates by category
Filter to only trade markets where the crowd is >X% off base
Discipline to accept variance on individual trades

name: Mean Reversion on Volatile Markets
description: Some markets swing wildly minute to minute, especially during live sports or election nights. When the price spikes far from where it was sitting and there's no real new information to justify it, you bet on it snapping back toward its recent average. The edge is that panic and overreaction push prices too far, then they revert. Because sometimes the move is real, tight stop-losses are critical so a genuine, information-driven move doesn't run you over.
requirements: Rolling volatility + midpoint calculation per market
Automated 'extreme move' detection vs. news tagging
Tight stop-loss rules in case the move was fundamental

name: Momentum / Trend Following
description: Rather than fight a trend, you ride it: when a market's price has been moving steadily one direction and breaks out of its recent range, you enter in that direction and let it run, exiting when it reverses. The edge is that prediction-market prices often keep drifting the same way as news and money continue to flow in, rather than turning on a dime. A trailing stop locks in gains and gets you out fast when momentum flips.
requirements: Price time-series storage with rolling-window indicators
Signal rules (e.g., N-minute breakout, volume confirmation)
Trailing stops to protect gains on fast reversals

name: Sports Analytics Model
description: You run a sports model (ELO ratings, the Massey method, or a machine-learning model) that outputs a win probability for each game, then trade whenever Polymarket's price differs from your model by more than a set threshold. The edge is having a calibrated probability the casual crowd lacks, applied across many games. Your model has to be good enough to beat the sharp sportsbook consensus, or the gap you're trading is just your own error.
requirements: Team/player-level dataset and trained win-probability model
Live injury, lineup, and weather feeds
Backtest showing the model beats consensus sportsbooks

name: Pair Trading
description: Buy one outcome and short a closely related one when the usual gap between their prices stretches too far (for example, 'Candidate A wins' should always trade below 'A's party wins', so if that gap widens abnormally you bet it snaps back). You make money on the spread converging back to its normal relationship, regardless of which way the overall market moves.
requirements: Pair selection based on historical price correlation
Z-score or cointegration model for entry/exit signals
Separate risk limits per pair and aggregate

name: Statistical Arbitrage Across Baskets
description: Group dozens of related markets into a basket (say, every 2027 gubernatorial race) and trade the basket against its expected aggregate outcome rather than betting on any single race. The edge: individually the markets are noisy, but in aggregate their combined probability should hit a stable number, so when the basket's total drifts away from your model you trade the whole group back toward it.
requirements: Pipeline to pull and normalize many market prices at once
Aggregate model with variance across the basket
Portfolio-level PnL attribution

name: Kelly-Optimal Sizing
description: Size each bet using the Kelly criterion, a formula that turns your estimated edge and the market's odds into the wager fraction that grows your bankroll fastest over the long run (in practice you use a fraction of full Kelly to soften swings). The point isn't picking winners but bet sizing: bigger when your edge is large, smaller when it's thin, so you compound efficiently without risking ruin.
requirements: Honest estimate of win probability for each bet
Script that converts edge + odds into a Kelly fraction
Bankroll tracking and drawdown limits

name: Dynamic Hedging / Gamma Scalping Analog
description: Hold offsetting Yes/No positions across correlated markets and keep rebalancing them as prices move, buying low and selling high on each swing while staying roughly market-neutral overall. Like gamma scalping in options, you profit from volatility itself rather than direction, as long as your rebalancing trades cost less than the swings they capture.
requirements: Real-time Greeks-style exposure model for binary payoffs
Automated rebalance trigger (price-move or time-based)
Cost model so rebalance frequency doesn't eat the edge

name: Adverse-Selection-Adjusted Spread Sizing
description: Each market's spread is set from how much it actually costs you to get adversely selected, measured as the average move against you right after a fill, plus the profit margin you want. So toxic, fast-moving markets get wider spreads and quiet ones get tighter spreads automatically. The edge is correctly pricing the risk you take on every quote across very different Polymarket markets, rather than using one fixed spread everywhere.
requirements: Historical fill markout dataset per market
Adverse-selection cost estimator (Glosten-Milgrom-style)
Dynamic per-market spread parameterization
Backtest harness on CLOB tape

name: Kalman-Filter Pairs on Cointegrated Outcome Tokens
description: Two outcome tokens that move together (e.g. two candidates in one primary, or BTC-above-X vs ETH-above-Y) usually trade at a stable price relationship. A Kalman filter is a running estimator that keeps re-fitting that relationship as new ticks arrive, so its ratio adapts faster than a fixed formula. You trade the spread between the two tokens whenever it drifts too far from the filter's current estimate, betting it snaps back. The edge: the on-chain order book is slow to reflect the true co-movement that the recursive estimate captures first.
requirements: Tick history per token to estimate state-space params
Kalman/Bayesian filter implementation with online beta update
Cointegration screening (Johansen/Engle-Granger) across token pairs
Capital to hold both legs plus inventory buffer

name: Hidden-Markov Regime Detection for Volatility Switching
description: A market tends to sit in one of two modes: 'quiet' (price barely moves, consensus is sticky) or 'jumpy' (news hits and it reprices fast). A hidden-Markov model is a statistical tool that infers which hidden mode a market is in right now from its recent price behavior. You then switch tactics by mode — bet on mean-reversion in quiet phases, ride the trend in jumpy phases. The edge is detecting the mode flip before the crowd adjusts.
requirements: Per-market price/volume time series at minute granularity
HMM/regime-switching model with online state inference
Backtest harness mapping regime to strategy/sizing
Execution code to flip posture on regime change

name: Ensemble Forecast vs Market-Implied Edge
description: Run several independent forecasting models on the same event — an Elo rating, a polling model, a fundamentals model, a machine-learning classifier — and average them into one combined probability, sizing your bet by how far that blended number sits from the market price. The edge is that averaging multiple models cancels out each one's errors, giving a sharper estimate than the single public model the crowd tends to anchor on.
requirements: 3+ independent forecasting models per market domain
Out-of-sample stacking/weight-optimization pipeline
Calibration check (reliability curve) before sizing
Automated quote ingestion to compute model-vs-market gap

name: Brier-Score Calibration Harvesting
description: Across thousands of resolved markets, check whether prices are accurate on average — for example, do 90-cent favorites actually win 90% of the time, or only 87%? Where a whole price band is consistently mispriced, you take the favorable side across every market in that band, not on any single opinion. The edge is a persistent, statistically measurable calibration bias in a price range, harvested in bulk so individual outcomes wash out.
requirements: Large resolved-market dataset with implied price at horizons
Reliability/calibration binning and Brier decomposition
Bucket-level position sizing across many markets
Ongoing recalibration as the bias decays

name: Probability Term-Structure Curve Trading
description: When one event is offered at many thresholds (e.g. BTC above 90k, 100k, 110k by the same date), the implied probabilities should fall in a smooth, consistent order. You fit a proper probability distribution to the whole ladder and trade any rung that's priced inconsistently with the others — for instance where a higher threshold is somehow priced more likely than a lower one. The edge is that the crowd prices each rung in isolation without enforcing a coherent overall curve.
requirements: Snapshot of all strike/date nodes in a ladder
Parametric distribution fit (lognormal/spline) to implied CDF
Detector for monotonicity/convexity violations
Multi-leg execution to lock the corrected curve

name: Order-Flow Imbalance Microstructure Model
description: Read the live order book to see whether buy pressure or sell pressure dominates right now — order-flow imbalance: how much size is stacked on each side, which way recent trades are hitting — and use it to predict the very next price tick, then trade ahead of that move. The edge is classic high-frequency microstructure trading applied to Polymarket's relatively unsophisticated book, where this imbalance signal strongly predicts short-term moves.
requirements: Full L2 book + trade-by-trade feed via CLOB API/WebSocket
Low-latency OFI feature computation and tick-ahead model
Sub-second execution with fee-aware thresholds
Risk caps on adverse-selection per market

name: RL Execution Agent for Order Slicing
description: Instead of dumping a large order into a thin book and moving the price against yourself, train an AI agent (reinforcement learning — it learns by trial and error in simulation) to break the order into smaller pieces placed at smart times, beating a simple even-spread (TWAP/VWAP) benchmark. The edge isn't a market view at all; it's cutting trading costs on Polymarket's thin books, which adds measurable profit to whatever signal you're already trading.
requirements: Market-replay simulator with realistic impact/fill model
RL training stack (env, reward = shortfall vs benchmark)
Live book state ingestion for inference
Guardrails/kill-switch on out-of-distribution book states

name: Bayesian Sequential-Update Probability Engine
description: Keep a running probability estimate for a market and formally update it (Bayesian updating — revise your belief by a set amount each time new evidence arrives) with every poll, stat, or on-chain signal, weighting each by how informative it is. When your updated estimate moves far enough from the market price, you trade. The edge is integrating many different kinds of evidence instantly and rigorously, while the market absorbs them piecemeal and slowly.
requirements: Prior elicitation + likelihood models per evidence type
Streaming evidence feeds normalized to update events
Posterior engine with credible-interval-based triggers
Position sizing tied to posterior-vs-market divergence

name: Volatility-of-Probability Trading
description: Track how MUCH a market's probability bounces around (its volatility), not just where it sits, and trade structures that pay off when that movement is mispriced: fade a market stuck near 50c that's about to break one way, or buy in cheaply before a known catalyst that will swing it. The edge is treating the size of probability swings as a tradable thing the binary yes/no crowd largely ignores.
requirements: High-frequency probability series to compute realized vol
Vol forecasting model (GARCH/EWMA) with catalyst calendar
Mapping from vol view to YES/NO entry/exit structure
Risk budgeting on path-dependent drawdown

name: Gradient-Boosted Resolution Classifier
description: Train a tree-based machine-learning model (gradient boosting — it combines many simple decision rules into one strong predictor) on features like market category, momentum, liquidity, who created it, and historical base rates, to estimate each market's true resolution probability. You then bet across every market where the model's number beats the price by a set margin. The edge is a data-driven signal that catches nonlinear patterns and feature combinations humans overlook.
requirements: Labeled dataset of resolved markets with rich features
Feature engineering + XGBoost/LightGBM training pipeline
Walk-forward validation and feature-stability monitoring
Cross-sectional portfolio construction with per-bet caps

name: Particle-Filter Nowcasting for Live Events
description: During a live event (a game, a vote count), use a particle filter — a method that keeps many guesses about the true state alive at once and reweights them as each new piece of noisy data arrives — to continuously estimate the real win probability, then trade the gap to the order book before it catches up. The edge is that this approach handles messy, partial live data better than the crowd's rough manual updates, and you act on it faster.
requirements: Streaming partial-observation feed for the live event
Particle-filter/state-space model of the underlying process
Sub-minute repricing and order placement loop
Latency edge over manual traders on the same feed

name: Cross-Sectional Factor Model on Markets
description: Rather than betting on single events, score every market by shared traits ('factors') like price momentum, liquidity, time left to resolution, and the favorite-longshot tilt, then go long the tokens those factors say are underpriced and short the ones they say are overpriced. The edge is harvesting systematic, repeatable factor premiums spread across hundreds of markets, so your return doesn't depend on any one outcome.
requirements: Panel dataset of market returns + factor exposures
Factor-return estimation (cross-sectional regression)
Market-neutral portfolio optimizer with constraints
Periodic rebalancing and factor-decay monitoring

name: Gaussian-Process Surface for Sparse Strike Markets
description: Threshold markets on the same theme (e.g. BTC above various prices and dates) are often priced thinly and inconsistently. A Gaussian process is a method that draws one smooth fair-value surface across the whole (price, time) grid AND reports how confident it is at each point. You trade any market sitting off that surface by more than the model's uncertainty allows. The edge is borrowing pricing information from related markets to value each thin one more accurately than its own sparse book can.
requirements: Cross-market quotes across strikes/expiries in a theme
GP regression with kernel tuned to event geometry
Uncertainty-aware trade triggers (posterior mean +/- sigma)
Execution across multiple illiquid nodes with size limits

name: Settlement-Latency Term-Structure Trade
description: The same real-world outcome can settle at different wall-clock times on different markets, because some use UMA's slower dispute window while others auto-resolve quickly. Pair a fast-settling and a slow-settling market on the same event and trade the implied financing gap between them, capturing the time-value of capital that's locked up longer in the slow leg. The edge is pricing that capital-lockup difference, which the market ignores.
requirements: Per-market settlement-mechanism + expected-liveness database
Same-event market pairing across resolution types
Discount-rate model for capital lockup duration
Capital allocator balancing both legs by settle-time

name: Resolution-Correlation Budgeted Sizing
description: This is a sizing rule, not a trade signal. Instead of treating each position as independent, map every market to its shared resolution drivers (the same election, the same crypto price level, the same UMA question family) and cap your total exposure to each underlying factor. The benefit is capital preservation: it stops the hidden concentration where 20 'diversified' bets are really one bet that all resolves off a single event.
requirements: Mapping of markets to shared resolution factors/oracles
Estimated correlation matrix from historical co-movement
Per-factor exposure cap + optimizer (mean-variance or risk-parity)
Position-level USDC accounting across the book

name: Volatility-Targeted Book Scaling
description: This is a sizing discipline, not a trade signal. Measure each held market's recent price volatility from the order-book midprice tape, then size positions so each one contributes roughly equal risk, and throttle the whole book's gross to hit a target overall volatility. The benefit is steadier returns and not being oversized in a market that has turned jumpy as it nears resolution.
requirements: Midprice tape ingestion per market
Rolling realized-vol estimator
Target portfolio vol + per-position vol-scaling logic
Automated resize/trim execution against the order book

name: Liquidity-Adjusted Position Limits
description: This is a position-limit rule, not a trade signal. Cap each position at a function of that market's order-book depth and recent volume (for example, max size = k times the depth within 3 cents of the mid), so your exit slippage stays bounded and no position can trap capital in a thin market. The benefit is avoiding the classic prediction-market mistake of taking size you can't unwind without crushing the price.
requirements: Live order-book depth + volume snapshots
Slippage/impact model from depth
Per-market size cap formula
Pre-trade limit check in execution path

name: Scenario/Stress Allocation Engine
description: This is a stress-testing allocator, not a trade signal. Define a handful of discrete macro scenarios (Fed cut, election flip, war escalation) and require the whole book's profit-and-loss under every one of them to stay inside a loss tolerance, only adding new capital where it improves the worst scenario. The benefit is a portfolio that survives across joint outcomes rather than one tuned to the single most-likely case.
requirements: Scenario set with per-market payoff mapping
Joint scenario P&L matrix across the book
Constrained optimizer minimizing worst-case loss
Capital-allocation interface to size new entries

name: Cross-Market Net-Exposure Netting
description: Add up your true directional bet on each underlying fact across every market at once, because a 'Yes' in one market can quietly offset a 'No' in a related one. You then only hedge or trade the leftover net amount instead of every gross position. The edge is capital efficiency and lower real risk: your books look big and scary but mostly cancel out, freeing cash that gross numbers tie up.
requirements: Shared-outcome mapping across related markets
Signed-delta aggregation per latent outcome
Residual-net hedging logic
Gross-vs-net capital tracking

name: Implied-Volatility Surface Import from Crypto Options
description: Use crypto options pricing from venues like Deribit to estimate the chance a coin finishes above or below a given price by a Polymarket market's expiry, then trade when Polymarket's implied probability disagrees with the options-implied one. IV surface just means the market's option prices across strikes and dates; the edge is a deep, always-priced derivatives market feeding a simple yes/no contract.
requirements: Live crypto options chain / IV surface (Deribit or equivalent)
Digital-option pricer converting surface to range probabilities
Expiry and strike alignment logic to the Polymarket contract
Funding/basis adjustment for spot vs perp reference price

name: Threshold-Cusp Gamma Harvest Near Strike Boundaries
description: Find threshold ('above X?') markets where the real-world number is sitting right at the resolution line late in the market's life, then trade the now-extreme price sensitivity as the number wobbles back and forth across the line, scalping each repricing. Digital gamma just means how violently the yes/no price swings per small move when you're near the boundary; that convexity gets sharper as resolution nears.
requirements: Live underlying value feed for the threshold variable
Digital-gamma model giving price sensitivity vs distance-to-strike
Low-cost rapid execution to scalp boundary oscillations
Stop logic for runaway moves away from the strike

name: Futures Basis & Term-Structure Import for Strike Markets
description: Dated futures trade above or below spot by an amount called basis, and the shape of that curve across expiries is the professional market's own forecast of where price will sit at each future date. You convert that curve into an implied distribution and compare it against Polymarket's 'will BTC close above $X on date Y' ladder. Where the ladder disagrees with the curve by more than fees, you take the side the curve supports — you are importing a deeper, better-capitalized market's opinion.
requirements: Dated futures and forward curves from CME plus a large offshore venue
Model converting basis + implied vol into a strike-by-strike probability
Fee-and-slippage threshold so only meaningful disagreements trigger

name: Token-Unlock Supply-Overhang Calendar
description: Most newer tokens release locked supply to teams and investors on a published vesting schedule, and a large unlock dumps sellable coins into the market on a known date. The size of the unlock relative to circulating supply and daily volume is the thing that matters — a 5% unlock into thin liquidity is a very different event from the same percentage into a deep book. You build the calendar ahead of time and position in price markets that straddle each unlock date.
requirements: Maintained unlock calendar with unlock size as a share of float and of daily volume
Historical study of price behavior into and out of comparable unlocks
Entry timing rules, since the anticipation often moves price before the date itself

name: Liquidation-Cascade Overshoot Fade
description: When leveraged positions get force-closed, each forced sale pushes price further and triggers the next one, producing a violent move driven by mechanics rather than news. Those cascades routinely overshoot and retrace a good portion within the hour. You detect the cascade in real time from liquidation prints and a volume spike with no accompanying headline, then fade the short-dated up/down market that has repriced with it. The essential discipline is separating a mechanical flush from a genuine information event.
requirements: Real-time liquidation feed plus volume and volatility spike detection
News-tagging cross-check so information-driven moves are excluded
Hard stop-loss, because a cascade sometimes is the start of a real trend

name: Cross-Coin Correlation Basket on Crypto Cycles
description: Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana move together most of the time, so their same-hour up/down markets should be priced as a correlated set rather than three independent coin flips. When one leg lags the others — say ETH is priced at 46% while BTC and SOL both sit at 55% with no coin-specific news — the set is internally inconsistent. You buy the lagging leg against the leaders and let the correlation reassert itself, which it usually does within the cycle.
requirements: Rolling correlation matrix across the coins that have paired cycle markets
Simultaneous quoting across all legs to avoid legging risk
Detection of genuine coin-specific news that legitimately breaks the correlation

name: Closing-Line Value Harvest
description: The closing line is the final price a sportsbook shows before a game starts, and decades of evidence say it is the single most accurate public forecast of the outcome. This strategy does not try to beat the closing line — it tries to beat the clock, buying Polymarket sides that the line is steadily moving toward and exiting once the line settles. You are effectively front-running a slow, well-documented convergence rather than making an independent prediction about the game.
requirements: Historical opening-to-closing line movement database across the leagues you trade
Live line feed from several books so you see the move as it forms, not after
Discipline to exit at the close rather than holding through the game

name: Weather-Adjusted Totals for Outdoor Games
description: Wind, rain and cold suppress scoring in outdoor sports in measurable, well-studied ways — a 20 mph crosswind is worth several runs in baseball and several points in football. Stadium-level forecasts update far more often than betting markets reprice. You pull a forecast for the exact venue, apply a scoring adjustment fitted on historical games in comparable conditions, and trade the total and outcome markets that have not moved with the weather.
requirements: Venue-level hourly forecast feed keyed to stadium coordinates
Regression of scoring outcomes on wind, precipitation and temperature by league and park
Rules for late forecast changes, which can reverse a position hours before kickoff

name: Live In-Game Win-Probability Divergence
description: A win-probability model fitted on historical play-by-play data can tell you what a 7-point lead with six minutes left is truly worth, and that number frequently differs from the live market, which overreacts to whatever just happened. You run the model against a live game-state feed and trade whenever the gap exceeds a threshold that covers fees. The hardest part is feed latency: if your data arrives later than everyone else's, you are the one being picked off.
requirements: Low-latency play-by-play or game-state feed, ideally faster than the broadcast
Win-probability model trained on historical in-game states for that sport
Latency measurement and an automatic stand-down when your feed falls behind

name: Rest, Travel & Schedule-Fatigue Model
description: Teams playing the second night of a back-to-back, or arriving after three time zones of travel, underperform their baseline by an amount you can measure across thousands of past games. This is a structural edge available weeks in advance because the schedule is public. You compute a fatigue score for every team on every date and trade the games where the market has not discounted a tired side, which happens most often in the mid-season stretch nobody is watching.
requirements: Full league schedule with travel distance, time-zone shifts and rest days per team
Historical performance regression on rest and travel variables
Sizing that respects how small each individual edge is — this is a volume strategy

name: Playoff-Seeding Combinatorial Tree Solver
description: Late-season 'will this team make the playoffs' markets depend on thousands of possible remaining-results combinations plus tiebreaker rules that most traders never read. You enumerate the remaining schedule by simulation, apply the league's actual tiebreakers exactly as written, and produce a clean qualification probability. The mispricing is largest for teams whose path depends on other teams' results, because the crowd prices the team's own record and stops there.
requirements: Monte Carlo simulator over the remaining schedule with per-game win probabilities
Exact implementation of the league's tiebreaker hierarchy, including head-to-head chains
Daily re-run as results land, since each night collapses large parts of the tree

name: Map-Pool & Veto Advantage Model
description: In games like CS2 the teams alternate banning maps, so the map that actually gets played is a predictable function of both teams' pools and the veto order. Teams have wildly different win rates by map — 70% on one, 40% on another — so knowing the likely map is most of the prediction. You simulate the veto sequence, weight by each map's historical head-to-head record, and trade series markets before the veto is public.
requirements: Per-team, per-map win-rate database kept current across recent patches
Veto-sequence simulator that respects the tournament's specific ban format
Fast update once the actual veto is published, which collapses the distribution

name: Live Objective & Gold-Lead Win Probability
description: MOBA matches expose a rich live game state — gold difference, tower count, dragon and baron control — and a model fitted on thousands of past games converts that state into a win probability far more reliably than eyeballing a stream. Live esports markets move on highlight moments, not on structural advantage. You consume the official match API and trade the gap, being careful that the API is ahead of the broadcast you are watching.
requirements: Official live match-state API access for the titles you trade
Win-probability model trained on historical game states for the current patch
Awareness of broadcast delay so you are trading against slower, stream-based traders

name: Bracket-Path & Group-Draw Model
description: Tournament winner markets frequently ignore the bracket: a strong team that must beat two other elite squads before the final is meaningfully less likely to win than an equally strong team on the soft side of the draw. You simulate the full bracket from seeding rules and per-matchup win rates, producing a title probability for every entrant, and trade the outright markets where the crowd priced team strength without pricing the path.
requirements: Bracket structure and seeding rules for the specific tournament format
Head-to-head matchup model feeding a full-tournament Monte Carlo simulation
Re-simulation after every round, since upsets reshape everyone's path

name: Ensemble-Spread Probability Trading
description: Weather agencies do not run one forecast — they run dozens of slightly perturbed versions, called an ensemble, and the spread between those members is itself the honest measure of uncertainty. Counting the fraction of members that clear a threshold gives you a directly tradeable probability. Markets quoted off a single headline forecast number ignore that distribution entirely, which is exactly where the mispricing sits.
requirements: Access to full ensemble member output (GEFS, ECMWF ENS) rather than just the deterministic run
Threshold-crossing counter that converts member outcomes into a probability
Bias correction per station, since raw model output is systematically off at some sites

name: Climatology Anchor for Long-Dated Weather
description: Beyond about two weeks, forecast models carry almost no skill, so the honest price for a distant weather market is the historical frequency adjusted for trend and for whatever El Niño-style pattern is in place. Long-dated weather markets nonetheless get bid around by recent conditions — a hot week in June moves an August contract that the weather in June tells you nothing about. You anchor to climatology and fade the recency.
requirements: Multi-decade station climatology with a warming-trend adjustment
ENSO and other seasonal-pattern overlays that genuinely shift the base rate
Patience to hold long-dated positions and ignore weather-driven noise in between

name: CPI Sub-Index Reconstruction
description: The headline inflation number is a weighted sum of components, and several of the heaviest ones — shelter, used cars, airfares, gasoline — can be estimated ahead of publication from private data that arrives much sooner. You rebuild the index bottom-up from those component estimates and compare your projection against the market's implied distribution before release day. The edge is that shelter alone is a third of the basket and follows rent data with a long, well-documented lag.
requirements: Component-level private data (rent indices, used-car auction prices, retail fuel prices)
Correct BLS weighting scheme and seasonal-adjustment handling
Track record of your own forecast errors, so position size reflects real accuracy

name: Payroll Revision Asymmetry
description: The monthly jobs report is revised twice after its initial release, and those revisions are not random — they cluster in one direction depending on where the economy is in the cycle, because the birth-death model for new businesses lags turning points. Markets that resolve on a revised figure, or that ask about a later comparison to an earlier print, can be traded on the revision pattern alone. You model the revision distribution rather than the headline.
requirements: Full vintage history of initial prints versus first and second revisions
Cycle-state classifier, since revision bias flips direction near turning points
Precise reading of whether each market resolves on the initial or revised figure

name: Jobless-Claims Seasonal-Factor Edge
description: Weekly unemployment claims are published seasonally adjusted, and the adjustment factors are known in advance and published by the agency. Around holidays, auto-plant retooling weeks and the start of school terms, the raw-to-adjusted conversion swings enough to move the printed number several thousand in either direction. You forecast the raw number from state-level filings, apply the published factor exactly, and trade the weekly threshold markets on the arithmetic.
requirements: State-level claims data plus the published seasonal-adjustment factor schedule
Calendar of the known distortion weeks for each year
Weekly execution cadence with small, repeatable position sizes

name: Earnings Whisper vs Consensus Beat Model
description: Published analyst consensus is a lagging, systematically conservative number — companies beat it roughly three quarters of the time — while the 'whisper' number circulating among buy-side desks is the figure the stock actually reacts to. Markets asking whether a company beats earnings are usually priced off the published consensus. You model the historical beat rate by company and sector, adjust for guidance history and revision momentum, and take the side the base rate supports.
requirements: Estimate-revision history and per-company beat/miss track record
Whisper-number sourcing plus sector-level surprise distributions
Precise reading of whether the market resolves on EPS, revenue or both

name: Index-Inclusion Committee Rule Model
description: Index additions look discretionary but run on published eligibility rules — profitability tests, float thresholds, seasoning periods, sector balance — and a committee that follows them closely. You maintain a scored candidate list against the actual rulebook, watch the quarterly rebalance calendar, and trade inclusion markets where the crowd is backing a famous name that fails a specific criterion. Ineligibility is often the whole trade, and it is checkable in advance.
requirements: Current index methodology document and a screener implementing each criterion
Rebalance calendar with announcement and effective dates
Float, liquidity and profitability data current enough to test eligibility

name: Precinct-Reporting Nowcast
description: On election night the raw vote total is deeply misleading, because precincts report in a non-random order — urban centers and mail batches often come late, producing a lead that predictably evaporates. A model that knows each precinct's historical partisan lean and expected turnout can convert partial returns into a projected final margin while the market is still reacting to the running total. This is the single largest recurring mispricing in political markets.
requirements: Precinct- and county-level historical results with expected-vote-share modeling
Live returns feed at county granularity, not just statewide totals
Uncertainty bands that widen appropriately when reporting patterns break from history

name: Early & Mail-Ballot Composition Model
description: In states that publish the party registration and demographics of everyone who has already voted, you can compute how much of each coalition's vote is already banked days before polls close. Comparing that composition against the same point in prior cycles gives a real, quantitative read on relative enthusiasm. Markets tend to trade on anecdote and turnout narratives while this hard data sits in a public file updated nightly.
requirements: Daily early-vote files by county with party registration and vote method
Prior-cycle baselines at the equivalent point in the calendar
Model translating banked-vote composition into an expected final margin

name: Seat-Level Fundamentals & Redistricting Model
description: For a House seat, the district's partisan lean, incumbency status and the national environment explain most of the outcome before any polling exists — and cheap, unpolled races are where markets are least efficient. When maps are redrawn, the old lean is obsolete and the market often keeps using it. You build a seat-level model from district composition and trade the many small races nobody bothers to price carefully.
requirements: District partisan-lean data updated for the current maps, plus incumbency and candidate quality
National-environment estimate feeding a uniform-swing-plus-noise model
Coverage across many low-liquidity races, since the edge is spread thin per seat

name: Candidate Drop-Out Hazard Model
description: Campaigns end for measurable reasons: money runs out, polling collapses below viability, staff depart, and the calendar reaches a state the candidate cannot win. Those inputs are all observable, and historical primaries give a clean base rate for exit timing given each condition. You build a survival model over the field and trade the nomination and drop-out markets, which routinely keep famous but non-viable candidates priced far above their real chance of continuing.
requirements: Campaign finance filings, staff-departure reports and polling trajectories per candidate
Survival model fitted on drop-out timing from past primary cycles
Delegate-math tracking to know when continuing becomes mathematically pointless

name: Special-Election Swing Benchmark
description: Special elections are held throughout the off-year, and the swing relative to each district's baseline lean has proven to be one of the better predictors of the next general election's national environment. Each result is a data point most traders ignore because the individual race is obscure. You compute the running average swing across all specials and use it to reprice the big national markets before the next round of polling arrives.
requirements: Comprehensive collection of special-election results including state legislative races
Baseline-lean computation per district so the swing is measured correctly
Historical mapping from cumulative special-election swing to eventual national results

name: Forecast-Model Consensus Gap
description: Several public election models publish daily probabilities using different methods — polls-only, polls-plus-fundamentals, and pure fundamentals — and their disagreements are informative. Markets tend to anchor on whichever model is being quoted in the news that week. You build a weighted consensus, weighting each model by its historical calibration rather than its popularity, and trade whenever the market drifts outside the ensemble's range.
requirements: Daily scraping of the public forecast models with a stored history of each
Calibration scoring of each model against past cycles to set the weights
Threshold rules so you trade only when the market leaves the ensemble band

name: Leader-Health & Succession Hazard Model
description: Markets on whether a head of state remains in office by a date are, at their floor, actuarial: age and known health conditions give a baseline hazard rate that can be computed from life tables. On top of that sits political risk. Long-dated versions of these markets frequently trade far away from the actuarial floor in both directions. You anchor on the mortality baseline, layer the political hazard, and trade the difference.
requirements: Actuarial life-table baseline by age, sex and country-specific mortality
Structured tracking of public appearances, absences and official health disclosures
Separate political-removal hazard estimate layered on the actuarial base

name: Instability & Coup-Risk Index
description: Political scientists have built and validated models of coup and civil-conflict risk from a consistent set of inputs: recent coup history, GDP shocks, army pay arrears, leader tenure and neighborhood contagion. Those inputs are publicly available, and the resulting base rates are far more informative than headline-driven intuition. You maintain the index across countries and trade the instability markets that are priced on news cycles rather than structural risk.
requirements: Country-level indicator panel covering economic, military and institutional risk factors
Model calibrated on the historical record of coups and irregular leader exits
Discipline about base rates, since these events are rare and easy to overprice after a headline

name: Speaker-Idiolect Frequency Model
description: Every public figure has a stable verbal fingerprint — how often they use a given word per thousand words, and in which settings. Given a corpus of their past speeches, the probability that a word appears in a speech of known length and topic is a straightforward statistical estimate. Markets tend to price these on vibes about the news cycle instead. You build the corpus once and price every mention market from it.
requirements: Transcript corpus per speaker, segmented by venue type and topic
Frequency model producing per-word appearance probability given speech length
Adjustment for current events that genuinely shift topic likelihood

name: Appearance-Calendar Base Rate
description: A market asking whether someone says something 'this week' depends first on how many opportunities they will have — rallies, interviews, hearings, posts — and only second on their vocabulary. The appearance calendar is largely public and highly predictable. You forecast the number of speaking opportunities in the window, combine it with a per-appearance mention rate, and price the market as a simple exposure calculation.
requirements: Maintained appearance calendar per figure, including recurring weekly commitments
Per-appearance mention rate by venue type from the historical corpus
Handling of cancellations and unscheduled appearances, which both move the count

name: Post-Volume Threshold Modeling
description: Markets asking how many times an account will post in a period are a counting process with strong daily and weekly rhythms plus occasional bursts. A model fitted on that account's history — typically a bursty Poisson process — prices the threshold far better than intuition, especially mid-window when part of the count is already banked. You track the running count live and reprice continuously as time runs out.
requirements: Complete posting history per account with time-of-day and day-of-week structure
Burst-aware counting model that handles clustered activity realistically
Live count tracking against the market's exact window boundaries and time zone

name: Box-Office Tracking & Opening-Weekend Model
description: Opening weekend is forecastable days ahead from presales, theater count, social interest and Thursday-preview grosses, and by Friday night the Saturday and Sunday multipliers are well-behaved enough to project the weekend total with tight error bars. Threshold markets are often still trading Wednesday's tracking estimate. You update the projection each night of the run and trade the residual.
requirements: Presale and daily-gross data plus theater-count and premium-format breakdowns
Weekend-multiplier model by genre and audience demographic
Fast update path Friday and Saturday nights as actuals replace estimates

name: Chart-Position & Streaming-Threshold Model
description: Chart positions are computed from a published formula combining streams, sales and radio spins, and the underlying streaming numbers are visible daily on the platforms themselves. That makes a number-one debut a calculation rather than a guess, several days before the chart posts. You track daily streams against the historical conversion into chart units and trade the chart markets during the tracking week.
requirements: Daily streaming counts across platforms plus sales and radio data
The current chart methodology, including stream-to-unit ratios by tier
Awareness of tracking-week boundaries and bundling rules that distort totals

name: Precursor-Award Signal Chain
description: Major awards arrive in a sequence, and the earlier ones are strong predictors of the later ones because the voting bodies overlap — the guild awards in particular have historically matched the eventual Oscar winner at a high rate in several categories. You build conditional probabilities from decades of precursor-to-final outcomes and reprice the outright markets after each precursor result, category by category, since the predictive strength differs sharply between them.
requirements: Historical precursor-to-final outcome database by award and category
Conditional model updating the outright probability after each precursor result
Category-specific weighting, since some precursors predict well and others barely at all

name: Announcement-Timing Pattern Model
description: Studios and labels announce on patterns: trailers drop a fixed number of weeks before release, tour dates go up on Tuesday mornings, and album announcements cluster around specific quarters. Markets asking whether something is announced by a date can be priced from those historical cadences plus observable pre-announcement traces like registered domains, trademark filings and venue holds. You model the cadence and trade the date markets.
requirements: Historical announcement-timing distributions by studio, label and franchise
Monitoring of trademark filings, domain registrations and venue availability holds
Calendar awareness of the industry events where announcements are traditionally made

name: Model-Release Cadence Hazard Model
description: Frontier AI labs ship on a rhythm you can measure: the gaps between their past releases, the lead time between a teaser and a launch, and the conference dates they like to land on. Markets asking whether a lab ships a model before a date are usually priced on the loudest recent rumor. You fit a hazard model to each lab's release history, layer in observable precursors, and price the date markets from the pattern instead.
requirements: Release-history database per lab with dates, gaps and pre-announcement lead times
Precursor monitoring: model cards, API string changes, staged documentation, job postings
Conference and event calendar, since launches cluster around specific dates

name: App-Ranking & Download Threshold Model
description: App store rank is a published function of recent download velocity, and third-party estimators publish daily download and revenue approximations. Markets asking whether an app hits number one or crosses a download milestone can be projected from the velocity curve, which has a very consistent shape after a launch or a viral moment. You track the curve daily and trade the milestone markets before the trajectory is obvious.
requirements: Daily rank and estimated-download data across the relevant stores and regions
Growth-curve model fitted on comparable past launches
Understanding of which estimator the market resolves against, since they disagree

name: Clinical-Trial Readout Probability
description: The chance a trial succeeds is well characterized by phase, therapeutic area and endpoint type — mid-stage oncology trials and late-stage cardiovascular trials have very different track records. Registry entries also disclose enrollment progress and expected completion, which tells you when the readout is coming. You combine the phase-specific base rate with the specific trial's design and trade the readout markets against a crowd trading the story of the disease.
requirements: Trial registry ingestion with enrollment status and primary completion dates
Phase- and indication-specific historical success rates
Endpoint analysis, since a change in the primary endpoint mid-trial is a meaningful signal

name: Epidemic Case-Curve Nowcast
description: Outbreak markets resolve on official counts that are published with a reporting lag and revised afterward, so the number that resolves the market is not the number visible today. Wastewater surveillance and test-positivity data lead confirmed cases by one to two weeks. You nowcast the reported figure by combining the leading indicators with the known reporting-delay distribution, and trade thresholds the raw dashboard understates.
requirements: Wastewater, test-positivity and hospitalization feeds alongside official case counts
Reporting-delay and revision model for the specific agency that resolves the market
Epidemic curve model translating current transmission into future reported counts

name: Realized-vs-Implied Volatility Cone for Cycles
description: An hourly up/down market prices the chance the coin ends higher, which is really a statement about how much it can move in the time remaining. Compare the volatility the market is implying against what the coin has actually realised over the same hour-of-day across recent weeks, and the gap is tradeable. Crypto has strong intraday volatility patterns — the US open and the Asia session are not the same market — and cycle pricing rarely reflects them.
requirements: Hour-of-day realized volatility history per coin, updated rolling
Conversion between an up/down price and its implied move for the time remaining
Session-aware calendar so weekend and holiday hours are modelled separately

name: Series-Length Distribution Model
description: Markets on whether a series goes the distance — 2-0 versus 2-1, or a deciding fifth map — depend on how evenly matched the teams are and on how much per-map results correlate within a series. Momentum is real in esports: the team that wins map one wins map two more often than independence would predict. You fit that correlation from historical series and price the length markets, which are usually quoted as if each map were an independent coin flip.
requirements: Historical series database with per-map results to estimate within-series correlation
Per-matchup map win probabilities feeding a series simulator
Separate parameters by format and title, since momentum differs between games

name: First-Freeze & Last-Frost Date Distribution
description: Seasonal-milestone markets — first freeze, last frost, first measurable snow — are questions about the date of a first crossing, and the historical record at a given station gives a tight distribution for that date. Overlay the seasonal pattern in play and a warming trend and you have a well-founded probability weeks ahead. These markets are usually priced off whatever the weather did last week, which has almost nothing to do with it.
requirements: Multi-decade station history of first- and last-occurrence dates
Trend and seasonal-pattern adjustments applied to the historical distribution
Conditional updating as the season advances without the event occurring

name: GDP Nowcast Tracker Blend
description: Several Federal Reserve banks run public GDP nowcasts that update automatically every time a component data point lands, and they routinely disagree with each other by a full percentage point because they weight the inputs differently. Their historical accuracy is measurable. You blend them by past performance rather than treating whichever one got quoted in the press as the truth, and trade growth and recession markets against the blended estimate.
requirements: Scraping of each public nowcast with a stored history of its revisions
Accuracy scoring of each tracker against final GDP prints to set blend weights
Understanding of which release each tracker reacts to, so jumps are anticipated

name: Analyst Revision-Momentum Factor
description: When analysts revise their estimates, they do it in herds and they do it slowly — an upward revision today makes another upward revision next week more likely, and that drift is one of the most durable documented effects in equity research. Markets on beats, guidance and price thresholds are priced on the current consensus, which by construction lags the revision trend. You trade the direction the revisions are moving, not the level they have reached.
requirements: Estimate-revision history at analyst level, not just the consensus average
Momentum measure capturing breadth and direction of recent revisions
Sector-relative normalisation, since revision cycles differ by industry

name: Conflict-Event Dataset Escalation Index
description: Academic conflict datasets code political violence event by event, with location, actor and fatality counts, updated weekly. That gives you a quantitative escalation curve instead of a vibe drawn from headlines — and headline volume and actual escalation diverge constantly, because coverage follows attention rather than events. You build the index and trade escalation and de-escalation markets against the measured trend.
requirements: Ingestion of a coded conflict-event dataset with weekly refresh
Escalation index combining event frequency, geographic spread and severity
Calibration against past episodes so index levels map to outcome probabilities

name: Multi-Word Bundle Joint Probability
description: Markets that ask whether a speaker says all of several words, or any of them, are joint-probability questions, and the words are strongly correlated — a speech that mentions tariffs almost certainly mentions China. Traders price these by multiplying independent guesses, which badly underprices the 'all of them' case and overprices 'any'. You estimate the correlation structure from the transcript corpus and trade the bundles against the naive independent price.
requirements: Co-occurrence statistics between target words across the speaker's past transcripts
Joint-probability model that respects correlation rather than assuming independence
Topic conditioning, since the correlation depends on the subject of the speech

name: S-Curve Adoption Model for Milestone Markets
description: Markets about a technology reaching a user, revenue or deployment milestone are questions about where a growth curve is on its trajectory. Technology adoption follows a well-studied S-shape — slow, then steep, then flattening — and fitting the curve to reported figures gives a far better date estimate than extrapolating the last quarter's growth rate. The crowd tends to extrapolate the steep middle forever, which overprices near-term milestones and underprices later ones.
requirements: Time series of the reported metric with a curve-fitting model and uncertainty bands
Comparable adoption curves from analogous technologies to constrain the fit
Careful reading of which reported figure the market resolves on

name: Uptake-Curve Model for Coverage Thresholds
description: Markets asking whether vaccination coverage, treatment uptake or screening rates clear a threshold by a date are curve-fitting problems with strong seasonal structure — uptake front-loads heavily in the first weeks of a campaign and then flattens to a long tail. Weekly reported figures let you fit the curve early and project the endpoint with tight bounds. Markets tend to extrapolate the steep early phase, which badly overprices high thresholds.
requirements: Weekly coverage reporting with the historical shape of comparable campaigns
Curve fit with saturation parameters and reporting-lag adjustment
Awareness of which agency figure resolves the market, since sources differ

name: Domain Expertise Edge
description: You pick one narrow area you genuinely know well (say crypto regulation, NBA injuries, or how bills move through Congress) and only trade markets in that lane. Your professional or insider-grade knowledge lets you price those specific markets better than generalist bettors who are guessing. The edge is informational depth in a narrow field, and you size up the trades where your conviction is highest.
requirements: Well-defined domain and list of relevant Polymarket categories
Personal research routine and sources (paywalled/insider OK)
Position-sizing framework that scales with conviction

name: Election-Night Live Trading
description: On election night you trade the race live as results come in, using your own county-level model that knows the expected vote share and reporting order for each area. When early returns look scary or rosy, you judge whether Polymarket is over- or under-reacting given which places have actually reported. The edge is interpreting partial returns faster and more accurately than the panicking crowd, which requires acting in seconds via a pre-built decision tree.
requirements: County-level model with expected vote shares and reporting order
Real-time scraping of AP/NYT/Decision Desk results
Pre-built decision tree so you can act in seconds, not minutes

name: Weather-Event Markets
description: For weather markets (hurricane track, temperature, snowfall), you use professional forecast models, including the ensemble runs from NWS and ECMWF that show a spread of likely outcomes, to estimate probabilities more precisely than casual bettors eyeballing the forecast. You map each forecast to the exact area and threshold the market resolves on, and update your position after every new model run. The edge is turning raw meteorological data into sharper odds.
requirements: Access to GFS/ECMWF ensemble data and a parsing pipeline
Geographic model mapping forecasts to market resolution zones
Rules for updating positions after each new model run

name: Earnings & Corporate Event Trading
description: For markets tied to specific companies (revenue beats, will-the-CEO-stay, will-a-merger-close), you dig into SEC filings, earnings-call transcripts, and what the options market is implying, to price the market more accurately than generalists. The edge is doing real financial homework on each catalyst and trading the gap between your estimate and the crowd's. A calendar of upcoming events per company tells you when each market is about to be decided.
requirements: EDGAR/transcript pipeline with NLP summarization
Options-market data for cross-reference pricing
Calendar of upcoming catalysts by ticker

name: Regulatory / Legal Calendar Trading
description: Keep a running calendar of scheduled regulatory and court decisions (FDA drug-approval deadlines known as PDUFA dates, Supreme Court opinion days, SEC ruling dates) and take a position before each one based on your read of the likely outcome. The edge comes from doing focused homework on a niche event most traders ignore, so you price the binary more accurately than the crowd before the ruling lands.
requirements: Maintained calendar of legal/regulatory events
Domain research sources (PACER, FDA.gov, SEC filings)
Exit plan for both favorable and adverse rulings

name: Legal-Outcome Specialist
description: Specialize in court and legal markets (Supreme Court rulings, indictments, verdicts) and price them more accurately than generalists by reading the actual filings, oral-argument transcripts, and precedent. Your edge is deep domain knowledge of how a given judge or panel tends to rule, letting you fade the crowd's headline-driven guesses.
requirements: PACER / court-listener subscription and monitoring
Law background or a legal consultant you trust
Catalog of past rulings per judge/panel for calibration

name: Macro / Fed Decision Trading
description: Trade Fed-decision, CPI, and jobs-report markets by comparing Polymarket's prices to the probabilities already baked into financial markets, like Fed funds futures (which imply the odds of a rate cut) and CPI swaps. When Polymarket drifts away from those professional benchmarks, you trade the gap, using Polymarket simply as the cheaper venue to express the same view.
requirements: CME FedWatch / fed-funds futures data feed
Economic-release calendar with exact timestamps
Script converting futures prices to binary probabilities

name: Geopolitical-Event Specialist
description: Focus on war, ceasefire, hostage, and treaty markets, pricing them ahead of mainstream news by mining open-source intelligence (OSINT) such as flight-tracking data, satellite imagery, and primary-language Telegram channels. The edge is information speed and access: you confirm developments from raw sources hours before reporters publish, and you need discipline given the grim subject matter.
requirements: Vetted OSINT source list with update discipline
Language coverage for primary-source reporting
Emotional discipline given the content of these markets

name: Crypto-Price Market Trading
description: For 'Bitcoin above $X by [date]' style markets, price the binary using the crypto options market's implied volatility and put/call skew (how expensive downside protection is versus upside bets). Those options reveal the market's true probability distribution for the price, letting you value the Polymarket binary more precisely than the crowd and trade when they disagree.
requirements: Deribit/CME options data for BTC/ETH
Black-Scholes (or model-free) probability calculator
Risk limits to avoid correlated blowups on crypto crashes

name: LLM-Assisted Research Workflow
description: Feed long source documents (bills, regulatory filings, court rulings, transcripts) to an LLM that summarizes them and surfaces markets where the document's implications aren't yet reflected in the price. The edge is reading speed at scale: the model digests material faster than competitors, flagging mispriced markets for a human to verify before trading.
requirements: LLM API access plus a document-ingest pipeline
Prompt library tuned per market category
Human review step before placing trades

name: Long-Term Thesis Holding
description: Ignore intraday noise entirely: buy into long-dated markets where you hold a strong multi-month thesis and hold to resolution, treating Polymarket as a conviction portfolio rather than a trading screen. The edge is patience and research depth; you tie up capital you won't need for months and re-underwrite the thesis only as major news arrives.
requirements: Well-documented thesis for each position
Capital you don't need for months
Review schedule to re-underwrite the thesis as news arrives

name: Awards-Voting Bloc Model (Oscars/Grammys)
description: Predict film and music awards from the precursor prizes that come first — SAG, DGA, PGA, BAFTA, Golden Globes — since these share many of the same voters and strongly foreshadow the eventual winner. You build win probabilities conditional on those precursor results and bet before Polymarket prices catch up. The edge is that casual bettors underweight how predictive a precursor sweep is in the weeks before the ceremony.
requirements: Historical precursor-to-Oscar/Grammy outcome dataset (20+ yrs)
Calendar of precursor announcement dates
Conditional-probability model keyed on guild overlaps
Bankroll staged across nomination-to-ceremony window

name: Space-Launch Slip & Scrub Modeling
description: Trade 'will it launch by date X' and 'will the launch succeed' rocket markets by modeling each provider's real-world track record of schedule slips and last-minute scrubs (SpaceX, ULA, Blue Origin, ISRO), plus weather windows and launch-range availability near the target date. The edge is that markets price too close to the published 'target' date, underestimating how often these programs slip and how long the delay tail runs.
requirements: Per-vehicle historical launch slip/scrub database
Launch-range weather and notam/TFR feeds
Static-fire and milestone tracking from provider feeds
Slip-distribution Monte Carlo model

name: AI-Benchmark Release Arbitrage
description: Trade 'will model X beat benchmark Y' and 'will model X ship by date Z' markets by tracking AI eval leaderboards (Chatbot Arena, MMLU, SWE-bench) and lab release patterns in near-real-time, plus pre-release API and leak signals from developer channels. The edge is that you see leaderboard jumps and credible leaks the moment they happen, while the market only reprices once mainstream coverage arrives.
requirements: Leaderboard scrapers (Arena, HF, SWE-bench, etc.)
Lab release-cadence and changelog tracking
Developer-forum/leak monitoring pipeline
Resolution-criteria parser per benchmark market

name: Nobel/Papal/Appointment Conclave Model
description: Trade pick-the-winner markets for Nobel Prizes, papal conclaves, and big appointments (Fed chair, Supreme Court, party leadership) using structured priors: citation rankings and prediction histories for Nobels, factional and geographic rotation patterns for conclaves, and shortlist leaks. The edge is that these patterns (Nobel field-rotation cycles, conclave kingmaker dynamics) let you price a crowded field of long-shot names that get little attention and are therefore mispriced.
requirements: Historical laureate/appointee outcome database with covariates
Citation/prediction (Clarivate-style) and oddsmaker shortlist data
Rotation/faction prior model per market type
Capital spread across multi-outcome candidate field

name: Tech Product-Launch Supply-Chain Signal
description: Trade 'will product X ship or be announced by date Y' markets (Apple events, GPU launches, console refreshes) by reading the breadcrumbs that precede an official announcement: FCC and other regulatory certifications, import shipping manifests, and the timing of press-event invites. The edge is that these public-but-obscure filings reliably leak a launch weeks before the keynote, so you can price the date correctly before the market reacts to the official reveal.
requirements: FCC/regulatory-filing and certification monitors
Import shipping-manifest (BoL) data subscription
Supply-chain leak/analyst-channel feeds
Launch-window probability model per product line

name: Scientific-Milestone Achievement Timing
description: Trade markets on science and engineering milestones (fusion net-energy-gain claims, quantum benchmarks, gene-therapy approvals, telescope first-light) by tracking the research pipeline that leads to them: arXiv/bioRxiv preprints, public grant and program roadmaps, and lab progress reports. The edge is turning that early technical flow into a realistic timing estimate before the milestone is confirmed by a press release, when the market is still pricing off vague hype.
requirements: arXiv/bioRxiv/program-roadmap ingestion
Domain-expert review of technical milestone definitions
Milestone-timing Bayesian model
Conference/announcement calendar tracking

name: Resolution-Rule NLP Mispricing Scanner
description: Use an AI to read every market's fine print, the resolution criteria plus the UMA oracle settlement language, at scale, and flag markets where the literal rules would resolve differently than the catchy title suggests (a specific cutoff date, a named source of truth, an edge-case clause). You take the side the crowd underprices because most people bet the headline, not the actual contract terms.
requirements: Structured ingestion of all market rule text + UMA ancestry
LLM parser fine-tuned/few-shot on past ambiguous resolutions
Database of historical rule-vs-outcome edge cases
Manual review queue for high-confidence flags

name: Automated UMA Dispute-Risk Forecaster
description: An AI reads each pending UMA oracle decision, the disputed evidence, and the size of the bond a proposer posted, then estimates the chance the proposed answer gets challenged or overturned before it becomes final. You trade markets where the public treats the proposed result as settled fact but the real dispute risk is mispriced.
requirements: UMA oracle event feed (proposals/disputes/bonds)
LLM trained on historical UMA dispute outcomes
Mapping of UMA assertions to Polymarket conditions
Capital reserved for slow dispute-window resolution

name: Judicial Docket & PACER Event Trader
description: Monitor federal and state court dockets, PACER/ECF electronic filings, and oral-argument calendars to anticipate when rulings, indictments, and verdicts will land, before mainstream news reports them. PACER is the US courts' public filing system; the edge is reading those filings plus knowing the procedure well enough to tell when a decision is imminent.
requirements: PACER/CourtListener docket ingestion with new-entry alerts
Procedural model mapping filing types to decision probability/timing
Calendar of argument and sentencing dates per tracked case
Legal-domain reviewer to interpret ambiguous entries

name: 60-Second TWAP Settlement Convergence Scalp
description: Polymarket's crypto cycles do not settle on the last tick you see on the ticker — they settle on a time-weighted average price (TWAP) taken over the final window, which smooths out the last-second wiggle. Because an average moves less than a spot price, the settlement value becomes highly predictable well before the cycle ends. You compute the running average yourself and trade any market still pricing as though a late spot spike could flip the result. The edge is that most of the book is watching the wrong number.
requirements: Sub-second price tape and your own rolling TWAP computed on the same window as settlement
Confirmed knowledge of the exact settlement window and source feed per market
Fast execution in the closing minutes, when spreads widen and size thins out

name: Stablecoin-Depeg Ladder Construction
description: Markets asking whether a stablecoin will trade below $0.99, $0.95 or $0.90 form a ladder of increasingly severe outcomes, and the prices along that ladder have to stay in order — a bigger break can never be more likely than a smaller one. Depegs are rare, so the crowd tends to underprice the shallow rungs and overpay for the dramatic ones. You track redemption queues, reserve attestations and on-chain pool imbalances, then buy the rung the plumbing supports while selling the rung that is priced on fear.
requirements: Reserve attestation and redemption-queue monitoring for each issuer
On-chain liquidity-pool imbalance tracking for the main stablecoin pairs
Ladder-coherence checks so the rungs stay in monotonic order

name: Protocol-Upgrade & Halving Countdown Drift
description: Network events like a Bitcoin halving or an Ethereum upgrade are scheduled by block height, not by clock time, so the exact date drifts as block times run fast or slow. Markets that ask whether an upgrade happens 'before' a given date are really asking a question about hash rate and block cadence. You project the arrival block from the trailing block-time average and trade the date markets that are still using the naive estimate everyone quoted months ago.
requirements: Live block-height and block-interval tracking with a projection model
Monitoring of client release schedules and testnet fork status for upgrades
Understanding of how each market's rules define the triggering event

name: Referee & Umpire Assignment Bias
description: Officials are not interchangeable: individual umpires have measurably tighter or looser strike zones, and individual referee crews call more or fewer fouls, which shifts scoring and pace. Assignments are published shortly before games and almost nobody prices them. You keep per-official historical splits, and when an extreme official draws a game whose total or outcome market is sensitive to pace, you take the side their history supports.
requirements: Per-official historical splits for scoring, fouls, penalties and pace
Assignment feed monitored for each league's publication time
Significance testing so small-sample officials aren't treated as signal

name: Tanking & Rest-Incentive Detection
description: Once a team is out of contention, its incentives invert: draft position beats winning, and stars start sitting for vague reasons. Coaches telegraph this in press conferences days before the market believes it. You track elimination status, draft-lottery positioning and coach language, then fade teams whose motivation has quietly evaporated — and equally, back teams still fighting for seeding against opponents who have already checked out.
requirements: Elimination and draft-position tracking across the league
Press-conference and beat-report monitoring for load-management language
Judgment about which rosters actually collapse without their starters

name: Patch-Note Meta Shift Model
description: Competitive games are re-balanced every few weeks, and a patch that buffs a character or weapon class immediately advantages the teams whose style depends on it. Patch notes are published days before they take effect in tournament play. You map each team's historical composition preferences against the changes and trade match and tournament markets before the field figures out who just got stronger.
requirements: Patch-note ingestion with a mapping from changes to affected picks and playstyles
Per-team composition history so you know who leans on what
Fast turnaround, since the advantage erodes as teams adapt within a week or two
