name: Hurricane Cone & Landfall Probability Model
description: Hurricane markets ask about landfall location, intensity at landfall, and named-storm counts, and the official forecast cone is a 2-in-3 confidence band, not a guarantee — a third of storms end up outside it. You build your own track distribution from ensemble spaghetti models and historical forecast-error statistics at each lead time, which lets you price the tails the cone visually understates. Intensity is far less predictable than track, and the markets often fail to reflect that asymmetry.
requirements: Official advisory ingestion plus ensemble track members at each update cycle
Historical forecast-error distributions by lead time for both track and intensity
Careful reading of landfall definitions, which vary by market and can hinge on a county line

name: Debt-Ceiling X-Date & Auction Calendar Model
description: The date the Treasury runs out of borrowing room — the X-date — is computable from daily cash balance and receipts data that the Treasury publishes every afternoon, plus the tax-collection calendar. Public estimates lag by weeks and cluster around round numbers. You rebuild the projection daily from the actual statement and trade the deadline and default markets whose prices still reflect a stale consensus estimate.
requirements: Daily Treasury Statement ingestion with a cash-flow projection model
Tax-receipt seasonality and extraordinary-measures accounting
Political calendar overlay, since the resolution is ultimately a legislative event

name: Shutdown Countdown Appropriations Tracker
description: Government shutdown markets resolve on a legislative deadline, and the real signal is procedural: which of the twelve appropriations bills have passed, whether a continuing resolution has been introduced, what the Rules Committee has scheduled, and how many days of floor time remain. All of that is public and structured. You track the procedural state machine rather than the cable-news temperature, and trade the countdown markets that price on rhetoric.
requirements: Congressional calendar and bill-status tracking via the legislative data APIs
Historical base rates for shutdowns conditioned on how far the process got by each date
Monitoring of leadership statements as a secondary, lower-weight signal

name: IPO Pricing & First-Day Pop Model
description: IPO markets ask whether a company lists by a date, prices above a range, or pops on day one, and each of those has a distinct, well-documented pattern: ranges get revised upward when demand is strong, and underwriters deliberately underprice to produce a first-day gain. The public signals are the S-1 amendments, range revisions and lockup terms. You track the filing trail and trade the listing markets on process evidence rather than on hype.
requirements: SEC filing monitoring for S-1/A amendments, range revisions and pricing terms
Historical distribution of first-day returns by sector and market conditions
Awareness of how delays and withdrawn deals resolve in each market's rules

name: Legislative Whip-Count Tracker
description: A bill passes when the votes are there, and most members announce their position publicly before the roll call. Maintaining a live count of declared yes, no and undecided votes turns a legislative market into an arithmetic problem with a small residual of genuine uncertainty. Markets often price the political narrative long after the count has become decisive one way or the other.
requirements: Structured tracking of member statements, cosponsorships and prior votes on similar bills
Legislative calendar and procedural gating (committee, cloture, rules) built into the model
Judgment about which undecideds historically break with leadership

name: Confirmation Vote-Math Model
description: Cabinet and judicial confirmations are a counting exercise inside a known chamber composition, with a handful of reliably independent votes who decide close cases. Their history on prior nominees is public and predictive. You model the chamber, weight the swing members by their record, and factor in the possibility of withdrawal — which is how many contested nominations actually end, and which some markets resolve differently from a failed vote.
requirements: Chamber composition with per-member confirmation voting history
Committee schedule tracking, since nominations die in committee more often than on the floor
Explicit handling of withdrawal versus rejection in each market's resolution rules

name: Endorsement-Cascade Network Model
description: Endorsements arrive in correlated waves: once a state's senior official commits, the delegation, county chairs and allied unions tend to follow within days. Treating endorsements as a network with known influence edges lets you forecast the next several before they happen. You trade nomination and primary markets on the leading indicator, entering when the first domino falls rather than after the cascade is visible to everyone.
requirements: Endorsement network graph with historical follow-on patterns by state and faction
Monitoring of official channels for endorsement announcements as they land
Weighting for which endorsements historically moved primary outcomes and which did not

name: Summit & Treaty Calendar Trade
description: Multilateral meetings — G7, G20, COP, NATO, OPEC — have fixed dates and a well-worn choreography: draft communiqués circulate to delegations days early, and outcomes leak through diplomatic press briefings. Markets asking whether an agreement is reached by a date are really asking whether the draft text survives the meeting. You track the drafts and the sherpa-level briefings rather than the summit coverage itself.
requirements: Calendar of upcoming summits with their formal agenda and decision items
Monitoring of delegation briefings, draft-text leaks and prior-summit precedent
Base rates for how often each forum actually produces binding outcomes

name: Missile-Test & Airspace-Notice Detection
description: Weapons tests are usually preceded by public administrative traces: navigational warnings closing a maritime area, NOTAMs restricting airspace, and afterwards seismic readings that confirm an underground detonation within minutes. All three are open data. You monitor them together and trade test-and-launch markets ahead of official announcements, which can lag by hours or be denied entirely.
requirements: Automated monitoring of NOTAMs, navigational warnings and public seismic networks
Geofencing around the known test sites and launch corridors of interest
Corroboration logic requiring two independent traces before acting

name: Reality-Format & Spoiler-Leak Trading
description: Competition shows are filmed well before broadcast, so the outcome already exists — and it leaks through spoiler communities, contestant social activity, filming-location sightings and promotional edits. Markets on these outcomes trade as if the result were still undetermined. You track the leak channels, weight them by their historical accuracy, and take positions on results that are functionally already known to a small group.
requirements: Monitoring of spoiler forums and social accounts with per-source accuracy scoring
Format knowledge, including how much of the outcome is decided by live voting
Skepticism about deliberate misdirection, which producers actively seed

name: Antitrust & Regulatory Docket Watch
description: Tech regulation markets resolve on filings and rulings that appear on public dockets before any press coverage: a scheduling order, a filed complaint, a designation under a digital-markets regime. Docket systems are pollable and timestamped. You watch the specific dockets tied to each open market and trade the moment a filing posts, which is routinely hours ahead of the story.
requirements: Automated docket polling for the relevant courts and regulators, including EU filings
Document classification to distinguish a procedural entry from a dispositive ruling
Legal-process knowledge to translate a filing into an outcome probability

name: PDUFA-Date Approval Calendar
description: Drug approvals run on a published clock: the FDA sets a target decision date for each application, and historical approval rates by review type, advisory-committee outcome and indication give a strong prior for what happens on that date. You maintain the calendar, weight each candidate by its trial results and committee vote, and trade the approval markets — including the meaningful probability of a delay rather than a decision, which markets often ignore entirely.
requirements: Maintained calendar of pending applications with their target decision dates
Historical approval rates conditioned on review pathway and committee vote
Explicit modeling of extensions and complete-response letters, not just approve/reject

name: Publication & Preprint Timing Model
description: Scientific milestone markets often resolve on publication in a peer-reviewed venue, and peer review has its own timetable measured in months, with conference deadlines and embargo dates that are public. A result can be complete and still miss a market's date because the journal pipeline is slow. You track preprint servers, conference acceptance lists and embargo schedules, and trade against markets that price the science while ignoring the publishing calendar.
requirements: Preprint server and conference acceptance monitoring in the relevant fields
Journal-specific review and publication lag statistics
Precise reading of what each market accepts as publication — preprint, journal or announcement

name: Regional Strength & Cross-Region Seeding Priors
description: Teams mostly play inside their own region, so their records are not directly comparable — a dominant record in a weak region means less than a middling one in a strong one. International events are the only place the regions meet, and those results give you a conversion factor between them. You maintain regional strength ratings from cross-region history and trade the early rounds of international events, where the crowd is pricing domestic records at face value.
requirements: Cross-region result history sufficient to estimate relative regional strength
Rating system that adjusts domestic records by their region's conversion factor
Awareness of roster and format changes that reset a region's strength

name: Prepared-Remarks Embargo Copy
description: Major speeches are distributed to press in advance under embargo — the State of the Union, central bank testimony, keynote addresses — and 'as prepared for delivery' text circulates among credentialed journalists before a word is spoken. Where that text is legitimately available, a mention market is not a prediction at all; it is a text search. The edge is knowing which events publish prepared remarks and which are improvised, where the base rate is all you have.
requirements: Knowledge of which event types release prepared remarks and through which channels
Text-matching against the market's exact phrase definition
Discount for improvisation, since speakers routinely depart from the prepared text

name: Space-Weather & Solar-Cycle Event Markets
description: Markets on geomagnetic storms, visible aurora at low latitudes and satellite disruption resolve on published index thresholds, and those indices are forecast by space-weather agencies from solar observations with one to three days of lead time. Active regions are tracked as they rotate across the solar disk, which gives a rhythm to the risk. This is a small, technical niche with almost no informed participation and fully public data.
requirements: Space-weather agency feeds for solar activity, coronal mass ejections and index forecasts
Understanding of the specific index and threshold each market resolves on
Solar-cycle context, since baseline event rates vary enormously across the cycle

name: Resolution-Criteria Hunting
description: Every market has fine-print rules saying exactly what makes it resolve Yes or No, and what source decides. This strategy reads that fine print closely and trades when the literal wording almost forces an outcome the crowd is mispricing because they're going on gut feel instead of the rules. The edge is interpreting the resolution criteria more precisely than everyone else. ('UMA' is the decentralized oracle that often settles these disputes, so knowing how it has ruled before helps.)
requirements: Careful read of every market's resolution source and rules
Log of past UMA/oracle rulings to predict edge-case behavior
Patience to wait for ambiguous markets to resolve

name: Long-Tail Decay Harvesting
description: Some markets sit at near-certain prices, like Yes shares trading under 1 cent or No shares above 99 cents, where the outcome is essentially decided but not yet final. You buy the near-certain side and hold to resolution to collect the tiny remaining premium, then repeat across many such markets so the small wins add up. The risk is that one of these 'sure things' surprises you, so you filter out any with a real catalyst that could flip them.
requirements: Large number of such markets running in parallel
Capital efficiency model (capital tied up vs. annualized yield)
Strict filter to exclude markets with tail-risk catalysts

name: Pre-Resolution Sniping
description: Sometimes an event is effectively over before the market officially closes: the game ends, the bill is signed, the race gets called. In that window, slow traders haven't updated and stale orders are still sitting on the wrong side. You watch the authoritative source in real time and sweep those leftover orders on the now-certain correct side before everyone else reacts. The edge is reaction speed plus a clear rule for what counts as 'decided.'
requirements: Monitoring of authoritative resolution sources in real time
Fast order routing to hit stale orders first
Clear playbook per market type for what counts as 'called'

name: Correlated-Market Hedging
description: You take the position you actually want in one market, then offset some of its risk by trading a related market that tends to move with it. If your main bet goes wrong, the hedge cushions the loss, so your drawdowns are smaller while you keep most of the upside of your core view. The trade-off is that hedging costs a bit of return ('drag'), so you only hedge when the protection is worth that cost.
requirements: Correlation matrix across candidate markets (rolling)
Hedge ratio calculation and rebalancing logic
Capital budget that accounts for hedge cost drag

name: Calendar / Time-Horizon Spread
description: When the same underlying question exists in short-dated and longer-dated versions ('Fed cuts in September' vs 'Fed cuts by year-end'), their prices must stay logically consistent, since anything that happens by September also happened by December. This strategy trades the two against each other when that term structure looks off, for instance if the by-year-end market is priced lower than the sooner one. The edge is the internal inconsistency across time horizons, not a view on the event itself.
requirements: Identification of nested/overlapping markets by theme
Term-structure consistency model
Willingness to hold through multiple resolution dates

name: Conditional-Market Trading
description: Conditional markets ask 'if X happens, does Y follow?' (e.g. 'if Newsom is the nominee, does he win?'). They give you a clean conditional probability that you can compare against the plain, unconditional markets using basic probability math: the chance of being nominee, times the chance of winning given the nomination, should equal the chance of winning outright. When those pieces don't multiply out correctly, you trade the legs against each other. The edge is the inconsistency between the conditional price and its parent markets.
requirements: Understanding of Bayes/conditional-probability math
Scanner for conditional markets and their unconditional parents
Capital to deploy across multi-leg positions

name: Thin-Liquidity Edge Mining
description: Big bots focus on popular, high-volume markets, so smaller obscure markets often have prices that stay wrong for a while because no one's correcting them. This strategy systematically crawls every live market, not just the featured ones, and grabs those lingering mispricings. Fills are small, so the play is to run a long tail of many tiny positions at once. You filter for enough depth to actually exit before entering.
requirements: Crawler that enumerates all live markets, not just featured ones
Filters for minimum depth so you can actually exit
Patience and a long tail of simultaneous small positions

name: Fat-Tail / Skew Trading
description: You buy very cheap Yes shares (say 3 cents) on rare events when you think the true odds are higher than the price implies (closer to 8%). Most of these bets lose, but the occasional winner pays off many times over, so the edge is being more accurate about small probabilities than the crowd. This only works with a big enough bankroll to survive long losing streaks and a written thesis for every longshot you take.
requirements: Rigorous base-rate and scenario modeling of rare events
Large enough bankroll to absorb long losing streaks
Written thesis for every low-probability bet opened

name: Cold-Start Market Edge
description: Trade brand-new markets in their first few hours of life, before informed traders arrive, when prices are still noisy and often badly mispriced. Your edge is having a fast fair-value estimate ready: you spot the gap between the sloppy opening price and a reasonable probability and take the cheap side before the market settles.
requirements: Alerting pipeline for newly listed markets
Pre-built priors for each market category you trade
Quick 'fair value' estimation workflow for first-look pricing

name: Dollar-Cost Averaging Into Long-Dated Markets
description: On a long-dated market where you hold a fundamental view, build the position gradually in small scheduled buys instead of all at once. This averages your entry price and cuts timing risk, so a single bad day doesn't define your cost basis, and a written rule tells you when thesis-breaking news should make you stop and exit.
requirements: Written thesis with target entry range
Scheduled buy plan (size, cadence, max total allocation)
Rule for when thesis-breaking news forces an exit

name: Synthetic 'Options' via Yes/No Structures
description: Combine Yes and No positions across several related price-threshold or scalar markets to build a custom payoff shape, mimicking options strategies like a bull spread (profit between two levels) or a condor (profit inside a range). Instead of a flat win/lose bet, you engineer where your gains peak, capping both risk and reward to match a specific view.
requirements: Multi-leg position management and PnL visualization
Understanding of payoff diagrams and break-evens
Sufficient liquidity in each leg to enter and exit

name: Catalyst-Window Positioning
description: Buy in a few days before a scheduled catalyst (a Fed meeting, jobs report, debate, or court ruling) while the market is still quiet, then exit soon after the result prints. The edge is that prices often sit sleepy ahead of known events and then move sharply; you capture that re-pricing with a clear time- or move-based exit.
requirements: Catalyst calendar with high-impact events tagged
Historical study of pre/post-catalyst price behavior
Clear exit rule (time-based or move-based)

name: Wash / Manipulation Detection
description: Detect markets being manipulated, by spotting suspicious volume spikes, wallets trading with themselves, or coordinated pump attempts, and respond by either steering clear or betting the manipulated price back toward fair value. The edge is on-chain forensics: clustering wallets and flagging abnormal volume/price combinations so you don't get run over and can fade fake moves.
requirements: On-chain trade graph analysis to identify clusters
Alerting on abnormal volume/price combinations
Clear rule to sit out if the market looks compromised

name: Portfolio Rebalancing Across Many Markets
description: Hold a portfolio of dozens to hundreds of small positions and rebalance regularly so no single outcome can blow up your book, using correlation-aware sizing. The edge isn't any one bet; it's diversification and risk control: by trimming correlated exposures and capping each name, you keep returns steady and survive bad runs.
requirements: Position and PnL database across all open markets
Correlation/covariance model for risk budgeting
Rebalancing rules that account for trading costs

name: Basket Strategy on Theme
description: Build a basket of markets that all express one thesis (for example, 'AI progress accelerates in 2026') and manage them together as a single portfolio instead of separate bets. The edge is conviction expressed broadly: if your thesis is right, multiple correlated markets pay off together, and weighting plus periodic rebalancing keeps the basket aligned with the view as news arrives.
requirements: Defined thesis and list of markets that express it
Weighting scheme (equal, conviction-based, or vol-based)
Thesis-update cadence and rebalancing rules

name: Negative-Risk Conversion Arbitrage
description: Polymarket bundles certain multi-candidate events as a 'neg-risk' group, which lets you trade all the NO shares as one unit. This strategy buys the NO share of every candidate in the group when their combined cost falls below what the protocol will pay to convert them. You then use Polymarket's NegRiskAdapter contract to merge those NOs into a single guaranteed payout, pocketing the gap between the cheap fragmented NO prices and the fixed conversion value.
requirements: NegRiskAdapter contract integration + ABI calls
Real-time per-leg NO ask prices for the event group
On-chain execution bot with conversion-cost accounting
Capital to hold all NO legs through conversion

name: USDC Bridge / Redemption Spread Arbitrage
description: A near-certain Polymarket share is guaranteed to redeem for $1 once the market settles, but settlement and moving cash off Polygon takes time. Some holders sell those shares below $1 just to get their money out instantly. This strategy buys from those impatient sellers and waits for the guaranteed $1 redemption. The edge is that people pay a premium for instant liquidity, and the cost of bridging funds off-chain is asymmetric.
requirements: Monitor of near-certain markets trading at a redemption discount
Bridge/withdrawal cost + timing model (Polygon to L1/exchanges)
Capital willing to hold to UMA finalization
On-chain order-flow detection of distressed sellers

name: Queue-Position Optimization at the Touch
description: On Polymarket's first-in-first-out order books, orders at a price level fill in the order they were placed. This strategy models where your order sits in that queue and times when to place or replace orders so you keep a good spot near the front, only joining a level when you're likely to get filled before the price moves against you. The edge is collecting more maker fills for the same risk by being early in line instead of chasing.
requirements: Order-book event reconstruction to infer queue depth ahead
Queue-aware placement/requote logic
Fill-probability model per level
Latency budget to maintain priority

name: Complement-Book Cross-Quoting
description: Because a YES share and a NO share always add to $1, buying YES is equivalent to selling NO (and vice versa). This strategy quotes both the YES and NO order books together, routing each maker order to whichever book offers a better spread or queue spot while keeping your net position flat. The edge is doubling the places you can provide liquidity and capturing differences between the two complementary books.
requirements: Simultaneous YES and NO order-book feeds
Complement-aware unified quoting engine
Mint/merge handling for share conversion
Joint inventory accounting across both tokens

name: Resolution-Drift Inventory Hedging for MMs
description: As a market maker's positions approach the oracle (UMA) resolution date, this strategy decides for each leftover position whether it's cheaper to simply hold it to settlement or to pair it with its complement and redeem it for $1 on-chain, based on remaining time value and gas costs. The edge is rescuing spread profits that careless makers lose to last-minute adverse trades and settlement uncertainty near expiry.
requirements: Time-to-resolution and oracle-status tracking per market
Settlement vs merge/redeem cost-comparison logic
Gas-aware on-chain redeem/merge execution
End-of-life quote-withdrawal scheduler

name: Multi-Outcome Awards Dutch-Book Construction
description: On award and entertainment markets with many mutually-exclusive candidates, add up the YES prices of every candidate. If they sum to more than 100% (an 'overround'), bet against the field; if they sum to less than 100% (an 'underround'), buy the whole basket of candidates, since one must win. The edge is that casual bettors price each name in isolation and never compute the cross-leg total, leaving these thin niche slates structurally mispriced.
requirements: Full order-book snapshots across all candidate legs
Overround/underround scanner with fee+slippage model
Multi-leg simultaneous execution bot
Capital to lock the full basket until resolution

name: UMA Dispute-Window Mispricing Capture
description: When a market enters UMA's oracle window (a proposed answer that anyone can dispute for a fixed 'liveness' period before it locks), the on-book price often still lags the now-obvious outcome. Buy the correct side at a discount and hold through the window, sizing for the small chance the proposed answer gets disputed and overturned. The edge is that many traders won't tie up capital during the multi-hour-to-days settlement lock, so they leave cheap shares behind.
requirements: UMA Optimistic Oracle event listener (OO contract proposals/disputes on Polygon)
Mapping of Polymarket questionID to UMA ancillary data + liveness timers
Capital tolerant of 2-7 day settlement lockup
Bond/dispute-history model to price re-dispute probability

name: Ambiguous-Resolution Cross-Venue Hedge
description: For markets whose resolution criteria are subjective or contested, take a side on Polymarket and hedge on another venue (Kalshi, a sportsbook, or another prediction market) whose rulebook would resolve the same event differently. If the two oracles disagree, your two positions net to a locked spread instead of a loss. The edge is that the market doesn't price the chance that two resolution sources read the same ambiguous event differently.
requirements: Rulebook diff database across venues for matched events
Accounts/liquidity on 2+ correlated venues
Legal/criteria-parsing workflow to flag ambiguous wording
Cross-venue margin and settlement-timing reconciliation

name: Expiry-Roll Re-Listing Edge
description: Recurring market series (weekly/monthly crypto-close or daily game markets) re-list a fresh contract on a predictable schedule, and the new listing often opens with lazy, uninformed quotes while the just-expired one still echoes its final price. Trade the gap between the stale roll and the cold-start fresh listing, anchored to the prior cycle's resolution history. The edge is the deterministic timing of re-listing plus the thin opening book.
requirements: Calendar of recurring market series + re-list timestamps
Historical resolution distribution per series
Auto-detection of new conditionId on re-list
Inventory model linking old/new contract carry

name: Redemption-Timing Float Harvest
description: After a market resolves, winning shares are redeemable for $1.00 each, but many holders are slow to click redeem and pay gas. Scan the leftover order book for resolved-but-unredeemed winning shares still trading below $1.00, buy them, and immediately redeem through the contract for the difference. The edge is pure holder inertia and gas-laziness leaving guaranteed-dollar shares on the book at a discount.
requirements: Post-resolution book scanner for sub-$1.00 winning tokens
ConditionalTokens redeemPositions automation
Low-latency Polygon execution with gas batching
Working capital recycled rapidly across many small claims

name: Fractional-Cent Rounding Edge
description: Polymarket displays prices in whole cents, but the underlying on-chain settlement uses 6-decimal USDC math. Systematically take fills where that rounding of size-times-price tips in your favor (buying just under a cent boundary, redeeming or merging at an exact $1.00) to skim sub-cent residuals, repeated at high volume. The edge is the quantization mismatch between the penny-tick display and the more precise on-chain settlement.
requirements: Exact replication of CLOB rounding/settlement arithmetic
High-frequency order submission infra under rate limits
Per-fill residual accounting to confirm positive skim
Bankroll sized for thin per-trade margin at volume

name: Dispute-Bond Asymmetry Positioning
description: When a UMA proposed answer looks wrong, the payoff to disputing it (you win the proposer's bond plus your correct market side) can exceed the bond you put at risk. Pre-position in the market for the post-dispute correction and, when your evidence is strong, actually post the dispute bond to force a re-vote. The edge is that almost no one plays the disputer role, so a well-researched dispute combined with a pre-built book position is underexploited.
requirements: UMA OO proposal monitor + ancillary-data resolver
Bond economics model (bond size vs market payoff vs win-prob)
Capital + UMA tokens to post dispute bonds
Evidence-gathering workflow for the dispute itself

name: Incentive-Cliff Liquidity Front-Run
description: Liquidity-mining and volume incentives create predictable behavior at the end of each reward epoch: LPs widen or pull their quotes and volume-farmers stop churning. Position just before the epoch boundary to capture the spread blow-out or to fade the wash-volume price impact, then exit. The edge is a calendar-deterministic microstructure distortion you can anticipate, not a view on the event itself.
requirements: Reward-epoch boundary calendar + historical end-epoch book behavior
Real-time depth/spread monitoring on incentivized markets
Pattern model for LP-pull vs volume-churn signatures
Fast execution to enter/exit around the cliff

name: Multi-Outcome Residual Long-Shot Sweep
description: In negRisk multi-candidate markets (where an adapter guarantees the set converts cleanly at resolution), the YES legs sometimes add up to less than $1.00, leaving a guaranteed residual, or a hopeless long-shot trades above the floor the adapter will pay it. Sweep the underpriced basket or short the over-floor tail, relying on the adapter's no-loss conversion guarantee. The edge is the structural floor/ceiling the adapter enforces, which thin tail legs violate.
requirements: Live Yes/No sum monitor across all legs of negRisk groups
NegRiskAdapter convert/redeem floor calculator
Batched multi-leg execution with gas netting
Capital to hold residual basket to resolution

name: Tail-Hedge Overlay via Cheap Long-Shot Legs
description: This is a risk-management overlay, not an alpha source. While running your core book of favorites and mean-reversion trades, continuously spend a small fixed budget on very cheap (sub-5c) shares on the disaster scenarios that would blow up that core. Those long-shot legs pay off big exactly when your main book is drawing down, so the cost is effectively insurance that smooths your equity curve through tail events.
requirements: Scenario mapping from core positions to disaster outcomes
Standing bids on cheap tail YES/NO legs
Premium-spend budget capped as % of book
Backtest of tail-leg payoff vs core drawdowns

name: Drawdown Circuit-Breaker Governor
description: This is a safety governor, not a trade signal. A supervisory layer watches your rolling peak-to-trough equity and automatically shrinks the whole book in tiers (for example, halve gross at -8%, stop all new entries at -15%), then locks out re-entry until a cool-down passes or equity recovers. The purpose is pure capital preservation: mechanically capping catastrophic losses when a model misfires or the market regime breaks.
requirements: Real-time mark-to-market equity feed
Tiered drawdown thresholds + state machine
Kill-switch wired to order cancellation/flatten
Cool-down and re-entry rules

name: Anti-Martingale Conviction Scaling
description: Scale into a position only as your thesis is proven right (add when the price moves toward your model's fair value) and cut size when it moves against you, the opposite of averaging down a loser. The edge is convex exposure: you get big on the trades that are working and stay small on the ones that aren't, which suits prediction markets since every market eventually settles to a clear yes-or-no truth.
requirements: Model fair-value estimate per market
Move-based add/trim ladder keyed to PnL/edge
Hard per-thesis loss cap
Execution that respects book depth on scale-ins

name: On-Chain Delta Hedge of Crypto-Price Markets
description: Cancel out the directional crypto risk in Polymarket price-threshold markets by holding an offsetting spot or perpetual-futures position elsewhere (for example, short an ETH perp against a long 'ETH above $X' YES). This isolates the prediction-market mispricing from the coin's price moves. The edge is harvesting the spread between Polymarket's implied probability and the derivatives market's, without betting on whether the coin itself goes up or down.
requirements: Delta estimate of each price-market vs underlying
Perp/spot venue with API (Polygon DEX or CEX)
Continuous rebalancing of hedge ratio
Cross-venue margin and basis-risk monitoring

name: UMA-Dispute Tail Reserve
description: Keep extra cash on the side and don't book a position at full value when a market's resolution wording is vague, until UMA's dispute window (the period in which the on-chain oracle's proposed answer can be challenged) has safely passed. You treat the chance of a contested or re-decided outcome as a discount on each position. The edge is surviving the occasional disputed resolution that wrecks anyone who sized as if the answer were already certain.
requirements: Resolution-text ambiguity scoring per market
Historical UMA dispute/delay base rates
Reserve sizing keyed to ambiguity score
Mark-to-model haircut applied to book equity

name: Gas/Settlement-Cost Aware Rebalancing Cadence
description: Treat Polygon network gas, exchange fees, and slippage as a spending budget, and only run a risk-control rebalance when the risk you remove is worth more than the round-trip cost, bundling small trims to stay under a monthly cost cap. The edge is preventing constant fiddling: over-frequent rebalancing quietly bleeds the account through fees even when each individual trade looks harmless.
requirements: Per-trade cost model (gas + fee + slippage)
Risk-improvement estimate per rebalance candidate
No-trade band / cost-budget threshold
Batched execution scheduler

name: Agentic Newsroom-to-Order Pipeline
description: A chain of AI agents reads raw newswire, RSS, and social feeds, decides which open Polymarket contracts each story actually affects, estimates how much it should move the probability, and fires a correctly-sized order within seconds. The edge is speed plus understanding: it reacts faster and reads the meaning of news more completely than simple keyword-matching bots.
requirements: Low-latency news/social feed subscriptions
LLM classifier mapping events to live market IDs
Auto-execution layer on CLOB with risk caps
Sub-second orchestration + dedup infra

name: Gas-Timed On-Chain Execution Optimizer
description: Bundle and time your settlements, redemptions, and large fills to hit Polygon's cheapest gas moments and least-congested blocks, predicted by a model watching the mempool (the queue of pending transactions). The edge is pure execution-cost savings: shaving fees and slippage off every trade adds up fast for high-frequency or large-size strategies.
requirements: Polygon mempool + base-fee monitoring feed
Gas-price forecasting model (intra-day seasonality)
Order-batching + nonce-management infra
Programmatic CLOB/redeem submission

name: LLM-Curated Stale-Quote Sweeper
description: An AI continuously summarizes the latest real-world facts for each market it tracks and spots resting limit orders that have gone stale, the trader behind them hasn't updated their price after fresh news. A fast executor grabs those mispriced orders before they get cancelled. The edge combines understanding when an order is out of date with the speed to take it.
requirements: Live order-book + cancel-rate monitoring
LLM event-state tracker per market
Sub-second take execution with mispricing threshold
News timestamp vs order-age correlation logic

name: Order-Routing MEV-Aware Fill Optimizer
description: Break a large order into smaller pieces and route them through private transaction channels (relays that hide your trade from the public mempool) so bots can't sandwich or front-run you on Polygon, while sequencing the child orders to minimize price impact. MEV is the profit those bots skim by reordering transactions; the edge here is keeping that money instead of leaking it to them.
requirements: Private relay / bundle submission access on Polygon
Order-slicing + impact-modeling engine
Mempool MEV-activity monitoring
Programmatic multi-fill CLOB execution

name: Notarized-Bridge & Wallet-Whitelist Settlement Race
description: Keep USDC pre-funded and your CTF and exchange spending permissions pre-approved so the moment one market resolves you can redeem the winnings and immediately redeploy that cash into a freshly mispriced market within the same low-gas window. CTF allowance is the on-chain permission Polymarket's contracts need to move your funds; pre-granting it removes a delay. The edge is compounding faster than traders stuck waiting on bridge transfers and approval steps.
requirements: Pre-funded, pre-approved wallets across CTF and exchange contracts
Automated redeem-then-redeploy router with gas-window timing
Pipeline of vetted mispriced targets ready to receive freed capital
Buffer reserve so redemption delays never force a forced sale

name: Spot-Ticker vs Oracle-Settlement Divergence Fade
description: The price shown on a market page and the price that actually resolves it can come from different places — one a live exchange ticker, the other an averaged oracle feed with its own update cadence. When the two drift apart, traders anchored to the visible ticker misprice the market relative to the thing that will actually settle it. You track both series continuously and take the side the resolution source supports. The whole edge is knowing precisely which number the contract obeys.
requirements: Simultaneous capture of the display ticker and the documented resolution feed
Alerting on divergence beyond a set basis-point band
Written confirmation of the resolution source in each market's rules before sizing up

name: Clinch & Elimination Certainty Trade
description: There is a moment in every season when a result becomes mathematically settled — a team has clinched or is eliminated regardless of what happens next — and markets often keep trading at 96 or 4 cents for hours or days afterward. You run the elimination math continuously against live standings and buy the certain side for a small but genuinely risk-free spread. It is a patience trade: capital is tied up until resolution, so the return is the annualized carry, not the headline percentage.
requirements: Live standings ingestion with automatic clinch and elimination detection
Careful reading of resolution rules for edge cases like forfeits and abandoned games
Capital planning, since funds sit locked until the market actually resolves

name: Stream-Delay Latency Guard
description: Esports broadcasts run 30 to 120 seconds behind the actual server state, and traders using the stream are effectively trading the past. If you are quoting or trading live esports markets without a direct data feed, you are the slow one, and you will be systematically picked off by anyone who is not. This strategy is the defensive discipline: measure your delay continuously, and either close the gap with an official feed or stop quoting during live play.
requirements: Continuous measurement of your own information delay versus the official match feed
Automatic quote withdrawal whenever your latency exceeds the safe threshold
Direct API access as the alternative to sitting out live windows entirely

name: Snowfall-Threshold Measurement-Site Specificity
description: Snow totals vary enormously across a single metro area, so a market asking whether a city gets six inches is really asking about one official measurement site — often an airport well outside the urban core. Traders picture the city; the contract measures a gauge. You model the specific site's microclimate and elevation, and you take the other side whenever the market is pricing the impression of the storm rather than the reading at that one location.
requirements: Identification of the exact official measurement site in each market's rules
Site-level snowfall history including the airport-versus-city-center bias
High-resolution model output rather than city-wide forecast summaries

name: Trace-Precipitation Resolution-Rule Edge
description: Precipitation markets hinge on definitions most traders never check: a 'trace' is recorded when there is measurable activity below 0.01 inches, and whether a trace counts as rain differs by market. Similarly, snow depth and liquid-equivalent are different measurements that resolve differently. You read each rulebook, identify markets whose price implies the wrong definition, and take the side that the written rule supports rather than the side the weather suggests.
requirements: Line-by-line reading of the resolution rules and their cited data source
Historical frequency of trace-versus-measurable events at the resolving station
Willingness to pass on markets whose rules are genuinely ambiguous

name: Recession-Definition Rulebook Trade
description: Recession markets look like macro bets but are mostly definition bets: some resolve on two consecutive quarters of negative GDP, others on the NBER committee's declaration, which arrives with a lag of six months to a year and weighs employment and income more heavily than GDP. Those two definitions can and have disagreed. You read which rule governs each market and trade the gap between markets that describe the same recession under different rules.
requirements: Exact resolution rule for every recession-related market you trade
Tracking of both the GDP series and the NBER committee's stated indicators
Comfort holding through a long declaration lag when the committee is the arbiter

name: Ballot-Access & Filing-Deadline Certainty
description: A candidate who has not filed by the statutory deadline, or who failed a signature challenge, cannot appear on the ballot — the question stops being political and becomes administrative. State filing deadlines and certification dates are published, and challenge rulings are public documents. You track the calendar and trade markets that are still pricing a candidacy the paperwork has already ruled out.
requirements: State-by-state filing deadline and certification calendar
Monitoring of secretary-of-state filings and signature-challenge dockets
Careful market-rule reading for write-in and third-party edge cases

name: Mention-Rule Ambiguity Mining
description: Mention markets are unusually rule-sensitive: does a repost count, does a plural or possessive form count, does a written post count for a market about speech, does the word inside a quoted headline count? The rules answer these, and the market price often does not reflect them. You read the resolution text closely, identify markets whose price implies a looser or stricter definition than the rules state, and take the side the text supports.
requirements: Systematic reading of resolution criteria including edge-case language
Precedent log of how similar ambiguities were resolved previously
Willingness to skip markets whose wording is genuinely unresolvable

name: Caption-Latency Arbitrage
description: The same live event reaches different audiences at different times: a raw satellite or press-pool feed can run 20 to 60 seconds ahead of the cable broadcast and further ahead of social clips. In mention markets, where resolution turns on a single moment, that gap is the entire game. You source the fastest legitimate feed available and, just as importantly, refuse to trade live when you know you are on the slow one.
requirements: Access to the earliest available live feed for the event type you trade
Continuous latency measurement against a reference to know where you stand
Automatic stand-down when your feed is behind, since being slow here is pure loss

name: Health-Statistic Revision Lag Trade
description: Public health statistics are provisional when first released and get revised for months as death certificates, lab confirmations and late reports come in — nearly always upward. A market resolving on the final figure while pricing off the provisional one is systematically mispriced in a known direction. You model the historical revision profile for each series and take the side the revision pattern favors.
requirements: Vintage history of provisional versus final figures for each statistical series
Revision-magnitude model by reporting lag and jurisdiction
Confirmation of whether each market resolves on the provisional or final release

name: Forfeit, Remake & Technical-Pause Rules
description: Esports matches break in ways traditional sports do not: a server crash forces a remake, a disconnect triggers a technical pause that can run an hour, a visa problem produces a walkover. How a market resolves in each case is in the rules and is frequently not what traders assume — a forfeited map may or may not count toward a handicap. You read the tournament ruleset alongside the market rules and trade the gap when a disruption is underway.
requirements: Tournament rulebook knowledge for remakes, forfeits, walkovers and pauses
Live monitoring of admin channels during disruptions, which is where rulings appear
Market-rule reading for how each disruption type resolves the contract

name: Corporate-Action Resolution Ambiguity
description: Price-threshold markets on individual companies assume the share price is a stable quantity, and corporate actions break that assumption: a stock split divides the price, a special dividend drops it, a ticker change or reverse merger can leave the referenced security ambiguous. Whether a market adjusts for these events is in its rules and often is not what traders assume. You watch the corporate-action calendar and trade the markets whose rules and whose price have quietly diverged.
requirements: Corporate-action calendar covering splits, spin-offs, special dividends and ticker changes
Line-by-line reading of each market's adjustment language, if any exists
Willingness to sit out markets whose rules simply do not address the action

name: Recognition & Definition Rules on Conflict Markets
description: The hardest part of a conflict market is rarely the geopolitics — it is the definition. What counts as an invasion, an occupation, a ceasefire holding, or formal recognition of a state is specified in the resolution text and is usually narrower than the everyday meaning. Many require a named body's declaration rather than events on the ground. You read the text, identify the markets pricing the news rather than the criterion, and take the side the rules support.
requirements: Close reading of resolution criteria and the specific sources they name
Tracking of the named arbiter bodies rather than general news coverage
Precedent log of how comparable definitional disputes were previously settled

name: Window-Boundary & Time-Zone Rules on Counts
description: A market asking how many times an account posts 'today' has to define today, and the definition is frequently ET while the account's activity clusters in another time zone — which moves a meaningful share of posts across the boundary. Deleted posts, edited posts and scheduled posts each have their own treatment in the rules. You read the boundary definition, count against it exactly, and trade the markets whose price reflects a different day than the contract does.
requirements: Exact window definition per market, including time zone and inclusive/exclusive endpoints
Counting infrastructure that timestamps against the contract's zone, not yours
Rules handling for deletions, edits and reposts, which differ market to market

name: Category Reclassification & Eligibility Rules
description: Awards bodies decide what competes where, and those decisions move markets more than the artistic merit does: a film submitted as a drama rather than a comedy faces a different field, a song's eligibility year hinges on release date, a series may be reclassified between limited and drama. The rules and submission deadlines are published, and rulings often land before the markets react. You track the eligibility process rather than the horse race.
requirements: Awards body rulebooks with submission deadlines and category definitions
Monitoring of eligibility rulings and submission announcements as they publish
Field-strength model, since reclassification changes who the competition is

name: Version-Numbering & Release-Definition Rules
description: A market asking whether a company 'releases' something has to say what counts, and in software almost nothing is clean: a limited preview, a staged rollout to 1% of users, a research paper with no weights, a paid early-access tier. Version numbering is equally slippery — companies ship point releases and renamed variants specifically to avoid a headline number. You read the definition and trade markets whose price assumes a looser one than the rules allow.
requirements: Resolution-text reading for what constitutes a release, and to whom
Tracking of staged-rollout and preview mechanics for each company
Precedent log for how prior ambiguous launches resolved

name: Record & Discovery Certification-Body Rules
description: Scientific and record-breaking markets usually resolve on a named certifying body rather than on the event itself: a temperature record must be ratified, a new element confirmed by a joint working party, an athletic record homologated. Ratification takes months and occasionally never happens, which means the event can occur and the market still resolve no. You read which body certifies, learn its timetable, and trade the gap between the achievement and its confirmation.
requirements: Identification of the certifying body and its ratification process for each market
Historical ratification timelines and rejection rates for comparable claims
Deadline awareness, since the market may expire before certification completes
